Nearby, a librarian helps a group of biology students use a database to search for recent studies about mammals. In the past few decades, the Internet has become an integral component of daily life for many people. The seemingly limitless power of search engines made the Internet search extremely common, and today people increasingly rely on the Internet’s vast accumulation of sources to access all types of information. Scientists are beginning to examine how this reliance is modifying the strategies people use to store and prioritize information in their mind.

lines.html: A Dependable and Valuable Asset
lines.text: A Dependable and Valuable Asset

lines.html: Psychologist Benjamin Storm from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and researchers Sean Stone and Aaron Benjamin devised an experiment to study students’ tendency to depend on the Internet for facts. To begin, the scientists divided sixty participants into multiple groups, including an “Internet” group and a “memory” group, and placed them in front of computers. The Internet group was required to use the search engine Google to answer eight challenging trivia questions. In contrast, participants in the memory group were permitted to use only their personal knowledge to answer the questions. In the second round, the researchers administered notably easier questions. This time, they allowed each group the option of using Google as they answered. Their results showed that 83 percent of the Internet group continued to consult Google in the second round, while only 63 percent of the memory group chose to do so.

The Internet group was required to use the search engine Google to answer eight challenging trivia questions. In contrast, participants in the memory group were permitted to use only their personal knowledge to answer the questions. In the second round, the researchers administered notably easier questions. This time, they allowed each group the option of using Google as they answered. Their results showed that 83 percent of the Internet group continued to consult Google in the second round, while only 63 percent of the memory group chose to do so.

lines.html: People’s growing inclination to rely on the Internet in order to retrieve information, particularly facts and figures, is called cognitive offloading. Canadian researcher Evan F. Risko and British researcher Sam Gilbert, who have written extensively about the topic, say a similar process has been taking place for centuries. In the past, people used resources like encyclopedias to assist their memories; however, today the Internet, serving as a vast extended memory, allows people to digitally access and retrieve much larger volumes of information. Consequently, people’s minds are free for other cognitive feats, such as connecting data, learning new information, or solving problems.

lines.html: The use of the Internet also appears to be modifying the strategies people use to store information in their mind. Researchers Betsy Sparrow from Columbia University, Jenny Liu from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and Daniel Wegner from Harvard University conducted several studies to discover how people efficiently manage their information intake.

Researchers Betsy Sparrow from Columbia University, Jenny Liu from the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and Daniel Wegner from Harvard University conducted several studies to discover how people efficiently manage their information intake.

lines.html: To begin, the researchers examined how people evaluate which information deserves their effort to remember. For this experiment, participants read forty trivia facts, such as “An ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain,” and typed the statements into a computer file. Half the participants had been previously told the file would be saved, while half believed it would be erased. Next, the participants wrote down every fact they could recall. Those who believed the information would be erased and no longer available could recall 40 percent more facts than those who thought the information would be saved.

For this experiment, participants read forty trivia facts, such as “An ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain,” and typed the statements into a computer file. Half the participants had been previously told the file would be saved, while half believed it would be erased. Next, the participants wrote down every fact they could recall. Those who believed the information would be erased and no longer available could recall 40 percent more facts than those who thought the information would be saved.

lines.html: In another experiment, the same researchers tested the ability of study participants to remember where to access information. For this trial, participants read and typed trivia statements, which they saved in folders with generic names such as “Facts” and “Items.” After spending ten minutes writing down all the facts they could recall from memory, participants were asked which folder contained a particular fact based on a keyword. For example, “Which folder has the fact about ostriches?” Overall, participants recalled the information’s location more often than the content itself, correctly identifying 49 percent of the folders for specific facts while remembering only 23 percent of the actual trivia. The researchers concluded that our memory is adapting to the Internet age by prioritizing where to locate information even when the specific details are forgotten. According to Sparrow, the Internet has become an important form of transactive memory, an external source of the recollections and associative networks that constitute memory.

According to Sparrow, the Internet has become an important form of transactive memory, an external source of the recollections and associative networks that constitute memory.

lines.html: As the Internet’s resources continue to expand our “external” memory, some question whether the process may cause people to depend too heavily on technology. However, Steven Pinker, a professor of psychology at Harvard University, says, “Knowledge is increasing exponentially; human brainpower and waking hours are not. Fortunately, the Internet and information technologies are helping us manage, search and retrieve our collective intellectual output at different scales, from Twitter and previews to e-books and online encyclopedias. Far from making us stupid, these technologies are the only things that will keep us smart.”

lines.text: Wolves of the Sea
lines.html: Wolves of the Sea

The cool and misty landscape of the Great Bear Rainforest can be found along the coast of British Columbia, Canada, and its nearby islands, from Vancouver Island to the Alaskan border. Within this protected area, wolves roam the forests, islands, and beaches. When biologist Chris Darimont began to study these wolves, he wanted to confer with local First Nations groups, as aboriginal Canadians are known, in order to learn what they knew about these wolves. He spoke with Chester Starr, an elder of the Heiltsuk Nation that has occupied the Great Bear Rainforest for thousands of years. What Starr had to say about the wolves changed Darimont’s perception of the animals.
lines.text: The cool and misty landscape of the Great Bear Rainforest can be found along the coast of British Columbia, Canada, and its nearby islands, from Vancouver Island to the Alaskan border. Within this protected area, wolves roam the forests, islands, and beaches. When biologist Chris Darimont began to study these wolves, he wanted to confer with local First Nations groups, as aboriginal Canadians are known, in order to learn what they knew about these wolves. He spoke with Chester Starr, an elder of the Heiltsuk Nation that has occupied the Great Bear Rainforest for thousands of years. What Starr had to say about the wolves changed Darimont’s perception of the animals.

lines.html: Starr asked Darimont which wolves he and his team were going to study—the timber wolves (mainland wolves) or the coastal wolves on the islands. The question took Darimont by surprise. Biologists had always believed that the wolves that are sometimes spotted swimming between islands and eating salmon are the same wolves that live on the mainland. Darimont was intrigued by Starr’s classification of the wolves as two different groups. At first, he was hesitant to accept the idea. The distances between the mainland and the islands are small, less than a mile. Why would the wolves on the islands be any different from the wolves on the mainland? To find out, Darimont and his research team studied the wolves on the islands and in the densely forested territory of the Great Bear Rainforest for ten years.
lines.text: Starr asked Darimont which wolves he and his team were going to study—the timber wolves (mainland wolves) or the coastal wolves on the islands. The question took Darimont by surprise. Biologists had always believed that the wolves that are sometimes spotted swimming between islands and eating salmon are the same wolves that live on the mainland. Darimont was intrigued by Starr’s classification of the wolves as two different groups. At first, he was hesitant to accept the idea. The distances between the mainland and the islands are small, less than a mile. Why would the wolves on the islands be any different from the wolves on the mainland? To find out, Darimont and his research team studied the wolves on the islands and in the densely forested territory of the Great Bear Rainforest for ten years.

lines.html: Throughout the study, Darimont recorded several significant, observable differences between the “sea wolves,” as they are nicknamed, and the mainland wolves. Compared with the mainland wolves, the sea wolves are smaller in size and are strong swimmers. In 1996 sea wolves were spotted on an island nearly eight miles from any other land formation. While mainland wolves almost exclusively eat meat, such as deer and elk, and teach their young to hunt for land animals, sea wolves get as much as 90 percent of their nutrition from the sea and teach their young to dig for clams and to catch fish. Sea wolves regularly swim between islands and have been known to sneak up on a seal sunning itself on a rock and make a leaping attack from the water. Some salmon-eating mainland wolves come and go from the islands with the fish-spawning season, but the sea wolves are full-time island residents. Darimont suspects that some sea wolves live their entire life on the islands.
lines.text: Throughout the study, Darimont recorded several significant, observable differences between the “sea wolves,” as they are nicknamed, and the mainland wolves. Compared with the mainland wolves, the sea wolves are smaller in size and are strong swimmers. In 1996 sea wolves were spotted on an island nearly eight miles from any other land formation. While mainland wolves almost exclusively eat meat, such as deer and elk, and teach their young to hunt for land animals, sea wolves get as much as 90 percent of their nutrition from the sea and teach their young to dig for clams and to catch fish. Sea wolves regularly swim between islands and have been known to sneak up on a seal sunning itself on a rock and make a leaping attack from the water. Some salmon-eating mainland wolves come and go from the islands with the fish-spawning season, but the sea wolves are full-time island residents. Darimont suspects that some sea wolves live their entire life on the islands.

lines.html: The sea wolves displayed not only physical and behavioral differences but also genetic variations from the mainland wolves. After collecting and analyzing the DNA in 800 samples of gray fur and wolf waste, researchers could produce hard biological evidence that sea wolves had genetic markers that made them distinct from the mainland wolves. A genetic marker is a variation in a DNA sequence that can be used to identify individuals or a species because it is passed down to offspring. Darimont hypothesizes that a change in habitat led to the eventual genetic differences between sea wolves and mainland wolves. Many years ago, loss of habitat and food sources forced some mainland wolves out to the islands. They learned to eat everything from kelp and fish eggs to the remains of sea creatures that washed up on the beach. Wolves living on the islands and mainland wolves became more isolated and rarely mated with each other. Over time the two types of wolves became more distinct.

lines.html: It turned out that Chester Starr was right all along. “It sounded totally bizarre at first,” admits Darimont, “that there could be two versions of the species.” But he now realizes that this skepticism “definitely reflected my ignorance of indigenous knowledge at the time.” Learning to trust the wisdom of the Heiltsuk people opened Darimont up to knowledge accumulated over millennia and positioned him so that he could gather new scientific evidence about one of British Columbia’s most elusive species, the sea wolf.

lines.html: Wolves of the Sea

The cool and misty landscape of the Great Bear Rainforest can be found along the coast of British Columbia, Canada, and its nearby islands, from Vancouver Island to the Alaskan border. Within this protected area, wolves roam the forests, islands, and beaches. When biologist Chris Darimont began to study these wolves, he wanted to confer with local First Nations groups, as aboriginal Canadians are known, in order to learn what they knew about these wolves. He spoke with Chester Starr, an elder of the Heiltsuk Nation that has occupied the Great Bear Rainforest for thousands of years. What Starr had to say about the wolves changed Darimont’s perception of the animals.

Within this protected area, wolves roam the forests, islands, and beaches. When biologist Chris Darimont began to study these wolves, he wanted to confer with local First Nations groups, as aboriginal Canadians are known, in order to learn what they knew about these wolves. He spoke with Chester Starr, an elder of the Heiltsuk Nation that has occupied the Great Bear Rainforest for thousands of years. What Starr had to say about the wolves changed Darimont’s perception of the animals.

lines.html: Starr asked Darimont which wolves he and his team were going to study—the timber wolves (mainland wolves) or the coastal wolves on the islands. The question took Darimont by surprise. Biologists had always believed that the wolves that are sometimes spotted swimming between islands and eating salmon are the same wolves that live on the mainland. Darimont was intrigued by Starr’s classification of the wolves as two different groups. At first, he was hesitant to accept the idea. The distances between the mainland and the islands are small, less than a mile. Why would the wolves on the islands be any different from the wolves on the mainland? To find out, Darimont and his research team studied the wolves on the islands and in the densely forested territory of the Great Bear Rainforest for ten years.

To find out, Darimont and his research team studied the wolves on the islands and in the densely forested territory of the Great Bear Rainforest for ten years.

lines.html: Throughout the study, Darimont recorded several significant, observable differences between the “sea wolves,” as they are nicknamed, and the mainland wolves. Compared with the mainland wolves, the sea wolves are smaller in size and are strong swimmers. In 1996 sea wolves were spotted on an island nearly eight miles from any other land formation. While mainland wolves almost exclusively eat meat, such as deer and elk, and teach their young to hunt for land animals, sea wolves get as much as 90 percent of their nutrition from the sea and teach their young to dig for clams and to catch fish. Sea wolves regularly swim between islands and have been known to sneak up on a seal sunning itself on a rock and make a leaping attack from the water. Some salmon-eating mainland wolves come and go from the islands with the fish-spawning season, but the sea wolves are full-time island residents. Darimont suspects that some sea wolves live their entire life on the islands.

lines.html: The sea wolves displayed not only physical and behavioral differences but also genetic variations from the mainland wolves. After collecting and analyzing the DNA in 800 samples of gray fur and wolf waste, researchers could produce hard biological evidence that sea wolves had genetic markers that made them distinct from the mainland wolves. A genetic marker is a variation in a DNA sequence that can be used to identify individuals or a species because it is passed down to offspring. Darimont hypothesizes that a change in habitat led to the eventual genetic differences between sea wolves and mainland wolves. Many years ago, loss of habitat and food sources forced some mainland wolves out to the islands. They learned to eat everything from kelp and fish eggs to the remains of sea creatures that washed up on the beach. Wolves living on the islands and mainland wolves became more isolated and rarely mated with each other. Over time the two types of wolves became more distinct.

While mainland wolves almost exclusively eat meat, such as deer and elk, and teach their young to hunt for land animals, sea wolves get as much as 90 percent of their nutrition from the sea and teach their young to dig for clams and to catch fish. Sea wolves regularly swim between islands and have been known to sneak up on a seal sunning itself on a rock and make a leaping attack from the water. Some salmon-eating mainland wolves come and go from the islands with the fish-spawning season, but the sea wolves are full-time island residents. Darimont suspects that some sea wolves live their entire life on the islands.

lines.html: The sea wolves displayed not only physical and behavioral differences but also genetic variations from the mainland wolves. After collecting and analyzing the DNA in 800 samples of gray fur and wolf waste, researchers could produce hard biological evidence that sea wolves had genetic markers that made them distinct from the mainland wolves. A genetic marker is a variation in a DNA sequence that can be used to identify individuals or a species because it is passed down to offspring. Darimont hypothesizes that a change in habitat led to the eventual genetic differences between sea wolves and mainland wolves. Many years ago, loss of habitat and food sources forced some mainland wolves out to the islands. They learned to eat everything from kelp and fish eggs to the remains of sea creatures that washed up on the beach. Wolves living on the islands and mainland wolves became more isolated and rarely mated with each other. Over time the two types of wolves became more distinct.

lines.html: It turned out that Chester Starr was right all along. “It sounded totally bizarre at first,” admits Darimont, “that there could be two versions of the species.” But he now realizes that this skepticism “definitely reflected my ignorance of indigenous knowledge at the time.” Learning to trust the wisdom of the Heiltsuk people opened Darimont up to knowledge accumulated over millennia and positioned him so that he could gather new scientific evidence about one of British Columbia’s most elusive species, the sea wolf.

Wolves of the Sea
lines.html: Wolves of the Sea

The cool and misty landscape of the Great Bear Rainforest can be found along the coast of British Columbia, Canada, and its nearby islands, from Vancouver Island to the Alaskan border. Within this protected area, wolves roam the forests, islands, and beaches. When biologist Chris Darimont began to study these wolves, he wanted to confer with local First Nations groups, as aboriginal Canadians are known, in order to learn what they knew about these wolves. He spoke with Chester Starr, an elder of the Heiltsuk Nation that has occupied the Great Bear Rainforest for thousands of years. What Starr had to say about the wolves changed Darimont’s perception of the animals.
lines.text: The cool and misty landscape of the Great Bear Rainforest can be found along the coast of British Columbia, Canada, and its nearby islands, from Vancouver Island to the Alaskan border. Within this protected area, wolves roam the forests, islands, and beaches. When biologist Chris Darimont began to study these wolves, he wanted to confer with local First Nations groups, as aboriginal Canadians are known, in order to learn what they knew about these wolves. He spoke with Chester Starr, an elder of the Heiltsuk Nation that has occupied the Great Bear Rainforest for thousands of years. What Starr had to say about the wolves changed Darimont’s perception of the animals.

lines.html: Starr asked Darimont which wolves he and his team were going to study—the timber wolves (mainland wolves) or the coastal wolves on the islands. The question took Darimont by surprise. Biologists had always believed that the wolves that are sometimes spotted swimming between islands and eating salmon are the same wolves that live on the mainland. Darimont was intrigued by Starr’s classification of the wolves as two different groups. At first, he was hesitant to accept the idea. The distances between the mainland and the islands are small, less than a mile. Why would the wolves on the islands be any different from the wolves on the mainland? To find out, Darimont and his research team studied the wolves on the islands and in the densely forested territory of the Great Bear Rainforest for ten years.

lines.text: Find Time to Volunteer
lines.html: Find Time to Volunteer

(1) Many people believe that they gain a greater sense of purpose by giving their time to serve others. (2) These are the people who spend their free time volunteering at various places within the community. (3) Those who are served benefit from the work of these volunteers. (4) However, research shows that those who volunteer also receive benefits.
lines.text: (1) Many people believe that they gain a greater sense of purpose by giving their time to serve others. (2) These are the people who spend their free time volunteering at various places within the community. (3) Those who are served benefit from the work of these volunteers. (4) However, research shows that those who volunteer also receive benefits.

lines.html: (5) For many students, this proposition may sound impossible. (6) Schoolwork can require hours of study each week. (7) Volunteering at a retirement center or homeless shelter requires both time and energy. (8) Extracurricular activities fill up after-school time. (10) However, if students can find time to volunteer, even for a few hours a month, they may find that the benefits outweigh the scheduling difficulties.

The question asks which revision of sentence 2 uses the most precise language.

A. CORRECT. In sentence 2, the author states that people who volunteer in their free time do so “at various places.” The revision to sentence 2 provides the most precise language because it references three specific places (animal shelters, community centers, and parks) where people often volunteer. B. Incorrect. Although this sentence mentions “a variety of places, events, or organizations” at which people volunteer, the revision does not use the most precise language, because it does not list specific places, events, or organizations. C. Incorrect. Although this sentence mentions “local establishments that help people, animals, or other groups,” the revision does not use the most precise language, because it does not name the specific types of establishments at which people can volunteer. D. Incorrect. Although this sentence mentions “places where [volunteers] can help people in many ways,” the revision does not use the most precise language, because it does not provide specific examples of where people can volunteer.

B. Incorrect. Although the sentence introduces the claim that “high school students should learn about” volunteering, it focuses on the idea that volunteering strengthens the community, which is not the main claim. This sentence does not accurately introduce the claim that volunteering is beneficial for high school students and thus should not follow sentence 4.

questions.explanation:
The question asks which sentence is least relevant to the ideas presented in the second

paragraph (sentences 5–10) and should be deleted.

A. Incorrect. Sentence 5 introduces the topic of the second paragraph, which is that finding time to volunteer “may sound impossible” for many students. Sentence 6 logically follows this idea because it provides one reason why students might hesitate or be unable to volunteer. Therefore, sentence 6 is relevant to the ideas presented in the second paragraph and should not be deleted. B. CORRECT. Sentence 7 states that “time and energy” are required for volunteering, which partially addresses the topic of the second paragraph about the various commitments that fill high school students’ schedules. However, sentence 7 interrupts the flow of the paragraph by interjecting specific examples (“volunteering at a retirement center or homeless shelter”) into a general list of activities and commitments. Thus, the sentence is the least relevant to the paragraph and should be deleted. C. Incorrect. In the second paragraph, the author discusses why some high school students may hesitate to volunteer. In sentences 6 and 9, the author points out that “schoolwork” and “family obligations and part-time jobs” are activities that require students’ time and may cause them to hesitate taking on any additional activities. Sentence 8 contributes to this idea by stating that “extracurricular activities” also require a time commitment from students. As a result, sentence 8 contributes to the ideas in the second paragraph and should not be deleted. D. Incorrect. In the second paragraph, the author acknowledges that some high school students may hesitate to volunteer because of “schoolwork” and “extracurricular activities.” Sentence 9 contributes to this idea by stating that “family obligations and part-time jobs” also require a time commitment and may cause students to hesitate to volunteer. Therefore, sentence 9 contributes to the ideas in the second paragraph and should not be deleted.

The subject of the main clause in sentence 12 is “admissions counselors.” Although the second sentence in the option mentions “admissions counselors,” it does not support the ideas in the paragraph, because the statement that “admissions counselors know that character traits like these will benefit the applicants” focuses on how students benefit, while sentence 12 focuses on how these traits benefit the community. B. Incorrect. While sentence 11 discusses the potential academic and professional connections that can be made through volunteering, sentence 12 moves on to the topic of college admissions. A. Incorrect. Although the sentence lists examples of organizations that depend on “hardworking young people” as volunteers, it should not replace sentence 22, because its use of specific examples does not provide a strong conclusion to the main idea in the passage, and it does not best support the main argument that students benefit themselves and their community when volunteering. B. Incorrect. While the sentence supports the argument that students “will experience a host of benefits” through volunteerism, it should not replace sentence 22 as a concluding sentence, because it does not best support the main argument that volunteerism benefits both the students and their community. C. Incorrect. Although the sentence emphasizes the importance of prioritizing volunteerism, it should not replace sentence 22, because it focuses on the main idea in the second paragraph (“For many students, this proposition may sound impossible.”), rather than the main argument that volunteerism benefits both students and their community. This sentence introduces the idea that student volunteers “are soon encouraging their peers” to volunteer, which does not best support the argument presented in the passage. D. CORRECT. This sentence should replace sentence 22 to conclude the passage because it lists specific reasons for volunteering (“Whether they are seeking admission to college, preparing to enter the workforce, or simply looking to reduce stress”) and best supports the main argument that volunteering not only helps students but can also help their community (“high school students who volunteer can help themselves as much as they help others”).

lines.text: In this excerpt from an 1819 short story, Rip Van Winkle, a good-natured but idle villager in colonial New York, has wandered into the Catskill Mountains on a squirrel-hunting trip.
Excerpt from “Rip Van Winkle”
by Washington Irving

lines.html: As he was about to descend, he heard a voice from a distance, hallooing: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” He looked round, but could see nothing but a crow winging its solitary flight across the mountain. He thought his fancy must have deceived him, and turned again to descend, when he heard the same cry ring through the still evening air: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” At the same time Wolf bristled up his back, and giving a low growl, skulked to his master’s side, looking fearfully down into the glen. Rip now felt a vague apprehension stealing over him; he looked anxiously in the same direction, and perceived a strange figure slowly toiling up the rocks, and bending under the weight of something he carried on his back. He was surprised to see any human being in this lonely and unfrequented place; but supposing it to be some one of the neighbourhood in need of his assistance, he hastened down to yield it.

He thought his fancy must have deceived him, and turned again to descend, when he heard the same cry ring through the still evening air: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” At the same time Wolf bristled up his back, and giving a low growl, skulked to his master’s side, looking fearfully down into the glen. Rip now felt a vague apprehension stealing over him; he looked anxiously in the same direction, and perceived a strange figure slowly toiling up the rocks, and bending under the weight of something he carried on his back. He was surprised to see any human being in this lonely and unfrequented place; but supposing it to be some one of the neighbourhood in need of his assistance, he hastened down to yield it.

lines.html: On nearer approach he was still more surprised at the singularity of the stranger’s appearance. He was a short, square-built old fellow, with thick bushy hair, and a grizzled beard. His dress was of the antique Dutch fashion: a cloth doublet strapped round the waist—several pair of breeches, the outer one of ample volume, decorated with rows of buttons down the sides, and bunches at the knees. He bore on his shoulder a stout keg, that seemed full of liquor, and made signs for Rip to approach and assist him with the load. Though rather shy and distrustful of his new acquaintance, Rip complied with his usual alacrity; and mutually relieving one another, they clambered up a narrow gully, apparently the dry bed of a mountain torrent. As they ascended, Rip every now and then heard long, rolling peals, like distant thunder, that seemed to issue out of a deep ravine, or rather cleft, between lofty rocks, toward which their ragged path conducted. He paused for an instant, but supposing it to be the muttering of one of those transient thunder-showers which often take place in mountain heights, he proceeded. Passing through the ravine, they came to a hollow, like a small amphitheatre, surrounded by perpendicular precipices, over the brinks of which impending trees shot their branches, so that you only caught glimpses of the azure sky and the bright evening cloud. During the whole time Rip and his companion had laboured on in silence; for though the former marvelled greatly what could be the object of carrying a keg of liquor up this wild mountain, yet there was something strange and incomprehensible about the unknown, that inspired awe and checked familiarity.

lines.html: On entering the amphitheatre, new objects of wonder presented themselves. On a level spot in the centre was a company of odd-looking personages playing at ninepins. They were dressed in a quaint, outlandish fashion; some wore short doublets, others jerkins, with long knives in their belts, and most of them had enormous breeches, of similar style with that of the guide’s. Their visages, too, were peculiar; one had a large beard, broad face, and small piggish eyes; the face of another seemed to consist entirely of nose, and was surmounted by a white sugar-loaf hat, set off with a little red cock’s tail. They all had beards, of various shapes and colours. There was one who seemed to be the commander. He was a stout old gentleman, with a weather-beaten countenance; he wore a laced doublet, broad belt and hanger, high-crowned hat and feather, red stockings, and high-heeled shoes, with roses in them. The whole group reminded Rip of the figures in an old Flemish painting, in the parlour of Dominie Van Shaick, the village parson, and which had been brought over from Holland at the time of the settlement.

lines.html: What seemed particularly odd to Rip was, that these folks were evidently amusing themselves, yet they maintained the gravest faces, the most mysterious silence, and were, withal, the most melancholy party of pleasure he had ever witnessed. Nothing interrupted the stillness of the scene but the noise of the balls, which, whenever they were rolled, echoed along the mountains like rumbling peals of thunder.

lines.html: As Rip and his companion approached them, they suddenly desisted from their play, and stared at him with such fixed, statue-like gaze, and such strange, uncouth, lack-lustre countenances, that his heart turned within him, and his knees smote together. His companion now emptied the contents of the keg into large flagons, and made signs to him to wait upon the company. lines.text: In this excerpt from an 1819 short story, Rip Van Winkle, a good-natured but idle villager in colonial New York, has wandered into the Catskill Mountains on a squirrel-hunting trip.
Excerpt from “Rip Van Winkle”
by Washington Irving

lines.html: As he was about to descend, he heard a voice from a distance, hallooing: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” He looked round, but could see nothing but a crow winging its solitary flight across the mountain. He thought his fancy must have deceived him, and turned again to descend, when he heard the same cry ring through the still evening air: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” At the same time Wolf bristled up his back, and giving a low growl, skulked to his master’s side, looking fearfully down into the glen. Rip now felt a vague apprehension stealing over him; he looked anxiously in the same direction, and perceived a strange figure slowly toiling up the rocks, and bending under the weight of something he carried on his back. He was surprised to see any human being in this lonely and unfrequented place; but supposing it to be some one of the neighbourhood in need of his assistance, he hastened down to yield it.

He was surprised to see any human being in this lonely and unfrequented place; but supposing it to be some one of the neighbourhood in need of his assistance, he hastened down to yield it.

lines.html: On nearer approach he was still more surprised at the singularity of the stranger’s appearance. He was a short, square-built old fellow, with thick bushy hair, and a grizzled beard. His dress was of the antique Dutch fashion: a cloth doublet strapped round the waist—several pair of breeches, the outer one of ample volume, decorated with rows of buttons down the sides, and bunches at the knees. He bore on his shoulder a stout keg, that seemed full of liquor, and made signs for Rip to approach and assist him with the load. Though rather shy and distrustful of his new acquaintance, Rip complied with his usual alacrity; and mutually relieving one another, they clambered up a narrow gully, apparently the dry bed of a mountain torrent. As they ascended, Rip every now and then heard long, rolling peals, like distant thunder, that seemed to issue out of a deep ravine, or rather cleft, between lofty rocks, toward which their ragged path conducted. He paused for an instant, but supposing it to be the muttering of one of those transient thunder-showers which often take place in mountain heights, he proceeded. Passing through the ravine, they came to a hollow, like a small amphitheatre, surrounded by perpendicular precipices, over the brinks of which impending trees shot their branches, so that you only caught glimpses of the azure sky and the bright evening cloud. During the whole time Rip and his companion had laboured on in silence; for though the former marvelled greatly what could be the object of carrying a keg of liquor up this wild mountain, yet there was something strange and incomprehensible about the unknown, that inspired awe and checked familiarity.

lines.html: On entering the amphitheatre, new objects of wonder presented themselves. On a level spot in the centre was a company of odd-looking personages playing at ninepins. They were dressed in a quaint, outlandish fashion; some wore short doublets, others jerkins, with long knives in their belts, and most of them had enormous breeches, of similar style with that of the guide’s. Their visages, too, were peculiar; one had a large beard, broad face, and small piggish eyes; the face of another seemed to consist entirely of nose, and was surmounted by a white sugar-loaf hat, set off with a little red cock’s tail. They all had beards, of various shapes and colours. There was one who seemed to be the commander. He was a stout old gentleman, with a weather-beaten countenance; he wore a laced doublet, broad belt and hanger, high-crowned hat and feather, red stockings, and high-heeled shoes, with roses in them. The whole group reminded Rip of the figures in an old Flemish painting, in the parlour of Dominie Van Shaick, the village parson, and which had been brought over from Holland at the time of the settlement.

He bore on his shoulder a stout keg, that seemed full of liquor, and made signs for Rip to approach and assist him with the load. Though rather shy and distrustful of his new acquaintance, Rip complied with his usual alacrity; and mutually relieving one another, they clambered up a narrow gully, apparently the dry bed of a mountain torrent. As they ascended, Rip every now and then heard long, rolling peals, like distant thunder, that seemed to issue out of a deep ravine, or rather cleft, between lofty rocks, toward which their ragged path conducted. He paused for an instant, but supposing it to be the muttering of one of those transient thunder-showers which often take place in mountain heights, he proceeded. Passing through the ravine, they came to a hollow, like a small amphitheatre, surrounded by perpendicular precipices, over the brinks of which impending trees shot their branches, so that you only caught glimpses of the azure sky and the bright evening cloud. During the whole time Rip and his companion had laboured on in silence; for though the former marvelled greatly what could be the object of carrying a keg of liquor up this wild mountain, yet there was something strange and incomprehensible about the unknown, that inspired awe and checked familiarity.

lines.html: On entering the amphitheatre, new objects of wonder presented themselves. On a level spot in the centre was a company of odd-looking personages playing at ninepins. They were dressed in a quaint, outlandish fashion; some wore short doublets, others jerkins, with long knives in their belts, and most of them had enormous breeches, of similar style with that of the guide’s. Their visages, too, were peculiar; one had a large beard, broad face, and small piggish eyes; the face of another seemed to consist entirely of nose, and was surmounted by a white sugar-loaf hat, set off with a little red cock’s tail. They all had beards, of various shapes and colours. There was one who seemed to be the commander. He was a stout old gentleman, with a weather-beaten countenance; he wore a laced doublet, broad belt and hanger, high-crowned hat and feather, red stockings, and high-heeled shoes, with roses in them. The whole group reminded Rip of the figures in an old Flemish painting, in the parlour of Dominie Van Shaick, the village parson, and which had been brought over from Holland at the time of the settlement.

lines.html: What seemed particularly odd to Rip was, that these folks were evidently amusing themselves, yet they maintained the gravest faces, the most mysterious silence, and were, withal, the most melancholy party of pleasure he had ever witnessed. Nothing interrupted the stillness of the scene but the noise of the balls, which, whenever they were rolled, echoed along the mountains like rumbling peals of thunder.

lines.html: By degrees Rip’s awe and apprehension subsided. He even ventured, when no eye was fixed upon him, to taste the beverage, which he found had much of the flavour of excellent Hollands. He was naturally a thirsty soul, and was soon tempted to repeat the draught. One taste provoked another; and he reiterated his visits to the flagon so often that at length his senses were overpowered, his eyes swam in his head, his head gradually declined, and he fell into a deep sleep.

In this excerpt from an 1819 short story, Rip Van Winkle, a good-natured but idle villager in colonial New York, has wandered into the Catskill Mountains on a squirrel-hunting trip.
Excerpt from “Rip Van Winkle”
by Washington Irving

lines.html: As he was about to descend, he heard a voice from a distance, hallooing: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” He looked round, but could see nothing but a crow winging its solitary flight across the mountain. He thought his fancy must have deceived him, and turned again to descend, when he heard the same cry ring through the still evening air: “Rip Van Winkle! Rip Van Winkle!” At the same time Wolf bristled up his back, and giving a low growl, skulked to his master’s side, looking fearfully down into the glen. Rip now felt a vague apprehension stealing over him; he looked anxiously in the same direction, and perceived a strange figure slowly toiling up the rocks, and bending under the weight of something he carried on his back. He was surprised to see any human being in this lonely and unfrequented place; but supposing it to be some one of the neighbourhood in need of his assistance, he hastened down to yield it.

lines.text: The following is adapted from an article by Priyanka Deol in the outdoors and infrastructure magazine Trailhead & Transit.
Excerpt from “Room to Roam”
by Priyanka Deol

lines.html: For decades, the stretch of the Trans-Canada Highway running through Banff National Park in Alberta was one of the deadliest roads in North America for wildlife. Elk, deer, and the occasional grizzly bear wandered onto the pavement at dusk, when headlights caught them too late for cars to stop. Collisions were common enough that highway crews kept a running count, and biologists worried that busy roads were quietly cutting large mammal populations into isolated, shrinking pockets, cut off from mates and food sources on the other side of the asphalt.
lines.text: For decades, the stretch of the Trans-Canada Highway running through Banff National Park in Alberta was one of the deadliest roads in North America for wildlife. Elk, deer, and the occasional grizzly bear wandered onto the pavement at dusk, when headlights caught them too late for cars to stop. Collisions were common enough that highway crews kept a running count, and biologists worried that busy roads were quietly cutting large mammal populations into isolated, shrinking pockets, cut off from mates and food sources on the other side of the asphalt.

lines.html: In 1996, Parks Canada tried something that had barely been attempted anywhere in the world at that scale: it began building bridges meant for animals, not cars. The structures, called wildlife overpasses, span the highway at points where animal trails already crossed, and each one is planted with the same grasses, shrubs, and soil found in the surrounding forest, so that from an animal’s point of view, the highway seems to disappear beneath a strip of ordinary hillside. Beneath the road, engineers added dozens of smaller underpasses, culverts and tunnels sized for foxes, badgers, and other animals that prefer not to climb.

lines.html: The results surprised even the biologists who had proposed the project. Camera traps installed at the crossings recorded more than eleven species using them within the first few years, including grizzly and black bears, wolves, cougars, moose, and lynx. Collisions between vehicles and large mammals in the park dropped by more than eighty percent in the areas where crossings were built, and highway planners in other mountainous regions began studying the Banff data as a model for their own roads.

lines.html: Not every animal adjusted at the same pace. Wolves and elk began using the new overpasses within months, but researchers found that grizzly bears, more cautious by nature, sometimes avoided a crossing for several years before an individual bear finally used it, after which the behavior seemed to spread through the local population, as though one animal’s confidence became a kind of instruction to the others. Biologists tracking bear movements with radio collars later confirmed something else the crossings were doing quietly, out of sight of the highway cameras: bears from populations on opposite sides of the road had begun to interbreed again after decades of separation, a change that geneticists could read directly in the cubs born in the years that followed.

lines.html: That genetic detail turned out to matter more than the collision numbers alone. A road wide and busy enough to stop animals from crossing does not just separate two groups of the same species for a season; over enough generations, it can split one healthy, genetically diverse population into two smaller, more vulnerable ones, each with a shrinking pool of possible mates. Wildlife biologists call this fragmentation, and reversing it, rather than merely reducing roadkill, is now considered the deeper purpose of a well-placed crossing.

lines.html: Building a single overpass is not cheap: current estimates run well into the millions of dollars once fencing, plantings, and monitoring equipment are included, and long stretches of fencing on either side of the road are needed to funnel animals toward the crossing rather than the traffic lanes. lines.html: In 1996, Parks Canada tried something that had barely been attempted anywhere in the world at that scale: it began building bridges meant for animals, not cars. The structures, called wildlife overpasses, span the highway at points where animal trails already crossed, and each one is planted with the same grasses, shrubs, and soil found in the surrounding forest, so that from an animal’s point of view, the highway seems to disappear beneath a strip of ordinary hillside. Beneath the road, engineers added dozens of smaller underpasses, culverts and tunnels sized for foxes, badgers, and other animals that prefer not to climb.

Camera traps installed at the crossings recorded more than eleven species using them within the first few years, including grizzly and black bears, wolves, cougars, moose, and lynx. Collisions between vehicles and large mammals in the park dropped by more than eighty percent in the areas where crossings were built, and highway planners in other mountainous regions began studying the Banff data as a model for their own roads.

lines.html: Not every animal adjusted at the same pace. lines.html: Engineers elsewhere have adapted the idea to local terrain: rope bridges strung through the forest canopy for tree-dwelling species in Australia, tunnels built specifically for salamanders in the northeastern United States, and even a much-photographed overpass in the Netherlands that carries wild boar and deer over a highway on a landscaped bridge nearly a thousand feet long. Not every wildlife crossing succeeds right away, and researchers caution that a poorly placed overpass, built where animals rarely traveled in the first place, can waste millions of dollars while doing little to reduce collisions. The Banff crossings work partly because biologists spent years studying existing animal trails before choosing where to build, rather than simply placing structures wherever construction was cheapest. That lesson, planners say, has become as important to export as the concrete and soil themselves: a wildlife crossing is only as good as the science that decided where to put it.

The following is adapted from an article by Priyanka Deol in the outdoors and infrastructure magazine Trailhead & Transit.
Excerpt from “Room to Roam”
by Priyanka Deol

lines.html: For decades, the stretch of the Trans-Canada Highway running through Banff National Park in Alberta was one of the deadliest roads in North America for wildlife. Elk, deer, and the occasional grizzly bear wandered onto the pavement at dusk, when headlights caught them too late for cars to stop. Collisions were common enough that highway crews kept a running count, and biologists worried that busy roads were quietly cutting large mammal populations into isolated, shrinking pockets, cut off from mates and food sources on the other side of the asphalt.

lines.html: In 1996, Parks Canada tried something that had barely been attempted anywhere in the world at that scale: it began building bridges meant for animals, not cars. The structures, called wildlife overpasses, span the highway at points where animal trails already crossed, and each one is planted with the same grasses, shrubs, and soil found in the surrounding forest, so that from an animal’s point of view, the highway seems to disappear beneath a strip of ordinary hillside. Beneath the road, engineers added dozens of smaller underpasses, culverts and tunnels sized for foxes, badgers, and other animals that prefer not to climb.

lines.html: The results surprised even the biologists who had proposed the project. Camera traps installed at the crossings recorded more than eleven species using them within the first few years, including grizzly and black bears, wolves, cougars, moose, and lynx. Collisions between vehicles and large mammals in the park dropped by more than eighty percent in the areas where crossings were built, and highway planners in other mountainous regions began studying the Banff data as a model for their own roads.

lines.html: Not every animal adjusted at the same pace. Wolves and elk began using the new overpasses within months, but researchers found that grizzly bears, more cautious by nature, sometimes avoided a crossing for several years before an individual bear finally used it, after which the behavior seemed to spread through the local population, as though one animal’s confidence became a kind of instruction to the others. Biologists tracking bear movements with radio collars later confirmed something else the crossings were doing quietly, out of sight of the highway cameras: bears from populations on opposite sides of the road had begun to interbreed again after decades of separation, a change that geneticists could read directly in the cubs born in the years that followed.

lines.html: That genetic detail turned out to matter more than the collision numbers alone. A road wide and busy enough to stop animals from crossing does not just separate two groups of the same species for a season; over enough generations, it can split one healthy, genetically diverse population into two smaller, more vulnerable ones, each with a shrinking pool of possible mates. Wildlife biologists call this fragmentation, and reversing it, rather than merely reducing roadkill, is now considered the deeper purpose of a well-placed crossing.

lines.text: The following is adapted from a local-history piece by Marcus Delfino for a New York City heritage newsletter.
Excerpt from “Message at the Speed of Air”
by Marcus Delfino

lines.html: Beneath the streets of Manhattan and Brooklyn, between 1897 and 1953, the United States Post Office ran a mail system that never touched a single delivery truck. Letters, driven by nothing but compressed air, shot through a network of iron pipes at speeds that could carry a bundle of mail from one end of the city to the other faster than a horse-drawn wagon could cross a single avenue.
lines.text: Beneath the streets of Manhattan and Brooklyn, between 1897 and 1953, the United States Post Office ran a mail system that never touched a single delivery truck. Letters, driven by nothing but compressed air, shot through a network of iron pipes at speeds that could carry a bundle of mail from one end of the city to the other faster than a horse-drawn wagon could cross a single avenue.

lines.html: The idea was not new when New York adopted it. European cities had experimented with pneumatic tube systems for telegrams decades earlier, and by the 1890s, engineers had scaled the technology up to carry heavier loads. Postal officials in New York, faced with a booming population and streets already clogged with delivery wagons, saw an opportunity: a network buried below the traffic, immune to weather, congestion, and the horse. Private companies won the early contracts, since the Post Office itself was reluctant to spend federal money on unproven equipment, and city officials only agreed to let crews dig up the streets after engineers demonstrated the system with a public test run watched by newspaper reporters.
lines.text: The idea was not new when New York adopted it. European cities had experimented with pneumatic tube systems for telegrams decades earlier, and by the 1890s, engineers had scaled the technology up to carry heavier loads. Postal officials in New York, faced with a booming population and streets already clogged with delivery wagons, saw an opportunity: a network buried below the traffic, immune to weather, congestion, and the horse. Private companies won the early contracts, since the Post Office itself was reluctant to spend federal money on unproven equipment, and city officials only agreed to let crews dig up the streets after engineers demonstrated the system with a public test run watched by newspaper reporters.

lines.html: At its largest, the New York system stretched across roughly twenty-seven miles of pipe connecting more than twenty post offices in Manhattan and Brooklyn. Cylindrical steel cartridges, each about two feet long and packed with as many as six hundred letters, were loaded at one station and pushed through the tubes by air pressure generated at powerful pumping plants along the route. A cartridge that might have taken an hour by wagon crossed Manhattan in under thirty minutes, and workers at each station could hear an incoming cartridge coming seconds before it arrived, giving them just enough time to catch it in a padded receiving box, sort its contents by hand, and route the letters onward to carriers waiting outside.

Cylindrical steel cartridges, each about two feet long and packed with as many as six hundred letters, were loaded at one station and pushed through the tubes by air pressure generated at powerful pumping plants along the route. A cartridge that might have taken an hour by wagon crossed Manhattan in under thirty minutes, and workers at each station could hear an incoming cartridge coming seconds before it arrived, giving them just enough time to catch it in a padded receiving box, sort its contents by hand, and route the letters onward to carriers waiting outside.

lines.html: The system became something of a public spectacle. Newspapers described the sound of a cartridge arriving at a station, and postal workers occasionally sent small items along with the mail; a photograph exists of a live cat, reportedly mailed as a publicity stunt, having survived a short trip through the tubes. Politicians and journalists were invited to watch cartridges launched on ceremonial first runs whenever a new stretch of tube opened, and for a brief stretch of the early twentieth century, a ride through the tubes was treated less like ordinary mail service and more like a demonstration of what the new century’s engineering could do.

Politicians and journalists were invited to watch cartridges launched on ceremonial first runs whenever a new stretch of tube opened, and for a brief stretch of the early twentieth century, a ride through the tubes was treated less like ordinary mail service and more like a demonstration of what the new century’s engineering could do.

lines.html: The tubes could not, however, keep pace with a changing city forever. Trucks became faster and more reliable, tunnel maintenance grew expensive as the iron pipes aged, and postal budgets tightened after two world wars. Critics inside the Post Office also pointed out that a single tube blockage could delay mail across an entire route at once, a risk that a fleet of trucks, able to take different streets, did not share. In 1953, the Post Office shut down the last of the pneumatic mail routes, and trucks took over the job the tubes had done for more than fifty years.

lines.html: New York was not the only American city to try the idea. Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago, and St. Louis each built their own pneumatic networks around the same period, moving mail between downtown post offices and outlying stations. None, however, matched New York’s system in scale or in the length of time it stayed in operation, and by the 1920s several of the smaller networks had already been abandoned in favor of trucks. New York’s tubes lasted decades longer partly because the city’s dense, traffic-choked streets made the underground alternative more valuable there than almost anywhere else in the country.

lines.html: Most of the tunnels remain underground today, sealed and forgotten beneath sidewalks and subway lines, a reminder that fast mail delivery has meant different things in different centuries, and that for one stretch of the twentieth century, the fastest way to send a letter across New York was to fire it through a pipe.

Trucks became faster and more reliable, tunnel maintenance grew expensive as the iron pipes aged, and postal budgets tightened after two world wars. Critics inside the Post Office also pointed out that a single tube blockage could delay mail across an entire route at once, a risk that a fleet of trucks, able to take different streets, did not share. In 1953, the Post Office shut down the last of the pneumatic mail routes, and trucks took over the job the tubes had done for more than fifty years.

lines.html: New York was not the only American city to try the idea. Philadelphia, Boston, Chicago, and St. Louis each built their own pneumatic networks around the same period, moving mail between downtown post offices and outlying stations. None, however, matched New York’s system in scale or in the length of time it stayed in operation, and by the 1920s several of the smaller networks had already been abandoned in favor of trucks. New York’s tubes lasted decades longer partly because the city’s dense, traffic-choked streets made the underground alternative more valuable there than almost anywhere else in the country.

lines.text: The following is adapted from a local-history piece by Marcus Delfino for a New York City heritage newsletter.
Excerpt from “Message at the Speed of Air”
by Marcus Delfino

lines.html: Beneath the streets of Manhattan and Brooklyn, between 1897 and 1953, the United States Post Office ran a mail system that never touched a single delivery truck. Letters, driven by nothing but compressed air, shot through a network of iron pipes at speeds that could carry a bundle of mail from one end of the city to the other faster than a horse-drawn wagon could cross a single avenue.
lines.text: Beneath the streets of Manhattan and Brooklyn, between 1897 and 1953, the United States Post Office ran a mail system that never touched a single delivery truck. Letters, driven by nothing but compressed air, shot through a network of iron pipes at speeds that could carry a bundle of mail from one end of the city to the other faster than a horse-drawn wagon could cross a single avenue.

lines.html: The idea was not new when New York adopted it. European cities had experimented with pneumatic tube systems for telegrams decades earlier, and by the 1890s, engineers had scaled the technology up to carry heavier loads. Postal officials in New York, faced with a booming population and streets already clogged with delivery wagons, saw an opportunity: a network buried below the traffic, immune to weather, congestion, and the horse. Private companies won the early contracts, since the Post Office itself was reluctant to spend federal money on unproven equipment, and city officials only agreed to let crews dig up the streets after engineers demonstrated the system with a public test run watched by newspaper reporters.

lines.html: At its largest, the New York system stretched across roughly twenty-seven miles of pipe connecting more than twenty post offices in Manhattan and Brooklyn. Cylindrical steel cartridges, each about two feet long and packed with as many as six hundred letters, were loaded at one station and pushed through the tubes by air pressure generated at powerful pumping plants along the route. A cartridge that might have taken an hour by wagon crossed Manhattan in under thirty minutes, and workers at each station could hear an incoming cartridge coming seconds before it arrived, giving them just enough time to catch it in a padded receiving box, sort its contents by hand, and route the letters onward to carriers waiting outside.

lines.html: The system became something of a public spectacle. Newspapers described the sound of a cartridge arriving at a station, and postal workers occasionally sent small items along with the mail; a photograph exists of a live cat, reportedly mailed as a publicity stunt, having survived a short trip through the tubes. Politicians and journalists were invited to watch cartridges launched on ceremonial first runs whenever a new stretch of tube opened, and for a brief stretch of the early twentieth century, a ride through the tubes was treated less like ordinary mail service and more like a demonstration of what the new century’s engineering could do.

passage.title: How a Mountain Becomes a Volcano

lines.text: The following is adapted from “About Volcanoes,” a public-domain publication of the U.S. Geological Survey’s Volcano Hazards Program.
How a Mountain Becomes a Volcano
by the U.S. Geological Survey Volcano Hazards Program

lines.html: More than fifteen hundred volcanoes around the world are considered potentially active, not counting the thousands more hidden beneath the ocean. In the United States alone, the U.S. Geological Survey monitors upward of one hundred sixty volcanoes that have erupted in the recent geologic past or show signs that they could erupt again. Roughly five hundred volcanoes worldwide have erupted at least once within the past hundred years, and a handful, including Hawaii’s Kilauea, have been erupting almost continuously for decades at a stretch.
lines.text: More than fifteen hundred volcanoes around the world are considered potentially active, not counting the thousands more hidden beneath the ocean. In the United States alone, the U.S. Geological Survey monitors upward of one hundred sixty volcanoes that have erupted in the recent geologic past or show signs that they could erupt again. Roughly five hundred volcanoes worldwide have erupted at least once within the past hundred years, and a handful, including Hawaii’s Kilauea, have been erupting almost continuously for decades at a stretch.

lines.html: A volcano begins with magma, molten rock that forms deep underground where temperatures and pressures are high enough to melt solid rock. Magma is less dense than the rock around it, so it works its way upward through cracks and weak points in the crust, sometimes pausing for years or centuries in an underground reservoir before moving again. Where it finally reaches the surface, at an opening called a vent, geologists no longer call it magma; once it breaks through, it becomes lava, along with clouds of ash, gas, and fragments of broken rock known collectively as tephra.
lines.text: A volcano begins with magma, molten rock that forms deep underground where temperatures and pressures are high enough to melt solid rock. Magma is less dense than the rock around it, so it works its way upward through cracks and weak points in the crust, sometimes pausing for years or centuries in an underground reservoir before moving again. Where it finally reaches the surface, at an opening called a vent, geologists no longer call it magma; once it breaks through, it becomes lava, along with clouds of ash, gas, and fragments of broken rock known collectively as tephra.

lines.html: Not every eruption looks the same, because the way magma escapes depends heavily on how much gas it holds and how easily it flows. Runny, gas-poor magma tends to pour out as smooth rivers of lava that spread for miles without much drama, allowing observers to approach far more closely than most people expect. Thicker, gas-rich magma behaves more like a shaken bottle: pressure builds until it is released all at once, blasting rock, ash, and gas high into the sky. The smallest ash particles from a powerful eruption can be thrown miles into the atmosphere and carried by high winds far beyond the volcano itself, sometimes circling the globe before finally settling, and even coating farmland and shutting down air travel thousands of miles from the eruption itself.

Thicker, gas-rich magma behaves more like a shaken bottle: pressure builds until it is released all at once, blasting rock, ash, and gas high into the sky. The smallest ash particles from a powerful eruption can be thrown miles into the atmosphere and carried by high winds far beyond the volcano itself, sometimes circling the globe before finally settling, and even coating farmland and shutting down air travel thousands of miles from the eruption itself.

lines.html: These different eruption styles build different shapes of mountain. A shield volcano, built from thin, fast-moving lava flows that travel far before cooling, ends up broad and gently sloped, like an ancient warrior’s shield laid flat on the ground; some shield volcanoes in the Cascade Range of California and Oregon rise fifteen hundred to two thousand feet high while spreading three to four miles wide at the base. A composite volcano, sometimes called a stratovolcano, is built from alternating layers of lava and tephra and tends to form the tall, steep-sided peaks most people picture when they hear the word volcano. A cinder cone, the simplest type, piles up quickly from a single short eruption of tephra around one vent and is rarely used again once that eruption ends, while a lava dome forms when thick, slow-moving magma piles up directly over a vent instead of flowing away from it; the lava dome that grew after Alaska’s 1912 Novarupta eruption reached roughly two hundred feet high and eight hundred feet across in a matter of months.

lines.html: The chart below compares the size of several of these features, from a modest lava dome to Ojos del Salado, a volcano on the border of Chile and Argentina that ranks among the tallest volcanoes on Earth at 22,615 feet above sea level, nearly a mile and a half taller than Mount Rainier in Washington State, which tops out at 14,410 feet and is itself one of the largest volcanoes in the continental United States. The comparison is a reminder that “volcano” describes an enormous range of landforms, from a dome barely as tall as a twenty-story building to a peak that pierces the clouds.

lines.html: Most of the world’s active volcanoes cluster along the edges of Earth’s tectonic plates, the enormous slabs of crust that slide, collide, and pull apart over millions of years. The Pacific Ocean is ringed by so many of these boundary volcanoes that geologists have nicknamed the pattern the “Ring of Fire,” a loose chain stretching from South America up through the western United States, across to Japan, and down through Southeast Asia. Not every volcano sits on a plate boundary, however; a smaller number, including the Hawaiian volcanoes, form instead over stationary plumes of heat rising from deep within the Earth, far from any boundary at all, which is part of why Kilauea’s activity looks so different from an explosive composite volcano thousands of miles away.

The Pacific Ocean is ringed by so many of these boundary volcanoes that geologists have nicknamed the pattern the “Ring of Fire,” a loose chain stretching from South America up through the western United States, across to Japan, and down through Southeast Asia. Not every volcano sits on a plate boundary, however; a smaller number, including the Hawaiian volcanoes, form instead over stationary plumes of heat rising from deep within the Earth, far from any boundary at all, which is part of why Kilauea’s activity looks so different from an explosive composite volcano thousands of miles away.

lines.html: Predicting exactly when a given volcano will erupt remains difficult, but scientists are rarely caught completely by surprise. Instruments buried near active volcanoes track subtle swelling of the ground, small earthquakes caused by moving magma, and changes in the gases escaping from vents, giving nearby communities days or weeks of warning before most major eruptions. That warning, built from decades of comparing one eruption to the next, is often the difference between a spectacular geological event and a genuine disaster, and it is why scientists continue to keep instruments running on volcanoes that have been silent for years, waiting for the small signs that come before the large ones.

lines.html: More than fifteen hundred volcanoes around the world are considered potentially active, not counting the thousands more hidden beneath the ocean. In the United States alone, the U.S. Geological Survey monitors upward of one hundred sixty volcanoes that have erupted in the recent geologic past or show signs that they could erupt again. Roughly five hundred volcanoes worldwide have erupted at least once within the past hundred years, and a handful, including Hawaii’s Kilauea, have been erupting almost continuously for decades at a stretch.

lines.html: A volcano begins with magma, molten rock that forms deep underground where temperatures and pressures are high enough to melt solid rock. Magma is less dense than the rock around it, so it works its way upward through cracks and weak points in the crust, sometimes pausing for years or centuries in an underground reservoir before moving again. Where it finally reaches the surface, at an opening called a vent, geologists no longer call it magma; once it breaks through, it becomes lava, along with clouds of ash, gas, and fragments of broken rock known collectively as tephra.

lines.html: Not every eruption looks the same, because the way magma escapes depends heavily on how much gas it holds and how easily it flows. Runny, gas-poor magma tends to pour out as smooth rivers of lava that spread for miles without much drama, allowing observers to approach far more closely than most people expect. Thicker, gas-rich magma behaves more like a shaken bottle: pressure builds until it is released all at once, blasting rock, ash, and gas high into the sky. The smallest ash particles from a powerful eruption can be thrown miles into the atmosphere and carried by high winds far beyond the volcano itself, sometimes circling the globe before finally settling, and even coating farmland and shutting down air travel thousands of miles from the eruption itself.

lines.html: These different eruption styles build different shapes of mountain. A shield volcano, built from thin, fast-moving lava flows that travel far before cooling, ends up broad and gently sloped, like an ancient warrior’s shield laid flat on the ground; some shield volcanoes in the Cascade Range of California and Oregon rise fifteen hundred to two thousand feet high while spreading three to four miles wide at the base. A composite volcano, sometimes called a stratovolcano, is built from alternating layers of lava and tephra and tends to form the tall, steep-sided peaks most people picture when they hear the word volcano. A cinder cone, the simplest type, piles up quickly from a single short eruption of tephra around one vent and is rarely used again once that eruption ends, while a lava dome forms when thick, slow-moving magma piles up directly over a vent instead of flowing away from it; the lava dome that grew after Alaska’s 1912 Novarupta eruption reached roughly two hundred feet high and eight hundred feet across in a matter of months.

lines.html: Most of the world’s active volcanoes cluster along the edges of Earth’s tectonic plates, the enormous slabs of crust that slide, collide, and pull apart over millions of years. lines.html: Predicting exactly when a given volcano will erupt remains difficult, but scientists are rarely caught completely by surprise. Instruments buried near active volcanoes track subtle swelling of the ground, small earthquakes caused by moving magma, and changes in the gases escaping from vents, giving nearby communities days or weeks of warning before most major eruptions. That warning, built from decades of comparing one eruption to the next, is often the difference between a spectacular geological event and a genuine disaster, and it is why scientists continue to keep instruments running on volcanoes that have been silent for years, waiting for the small signs that come before the large ones.

Runny, gas-poor magma tends to pour out as smooth rivers of lava that spread for miles without much drama, allowing observers to approach far more closely than most people expect. Thicker, gas-rich magma behaves more like a shaken bottle: pressure builds until it is released all at once, blasting rock, ash, and gas high into the sky. The smallest ash particles from a powerful eruption can be thrown miles into the atmosphere and carried by high winds far beyond the volcano itself, sometimes circling the globe before finally settling, and even coating farmland and shutting down air travel thousands of miles from the eruption itself.

lines.html: These different eruption styles build different shapes of mountain. A shield volcano, built from thin, fast-moving lava flows that travel far before cooling, ends up broad and gently sloped, like an ancient warrior’s shield laid flat on the ground; some shield volcanoes in the Cascade Range of California and Oregon rise fifteen hundred to two thousand feet high while spreading three to four miles wide at the base. A composite volcano, sometimes called a stratovolcano, is built from alternating layers of lava and tephra and tends to form the tall, steep-sided peaks most people picture when they hear the word volcano. A cinder cone, the simplest type, piles up quickly from a single short eruption of tephra around one vent and is rarely used again once that eruption ends, while a lava dome forms when thick, slow-moving magma piles up directly over a vent instead of flowing away from it; the lava dome that grew after Alaska’s 1912 Novarupta eruption reached roughly two hundred feet high and eight hundred feet across in a matter of months.

lines.html: Most of the world’s active volcanoes cluster along the edges of Earth’s tectonic plates, the enormous slabs of crust that slide, collide, and pull apart over millions of years. The Pacific Ocean is ringed by so many of these boundary volcanoes that geologists have nicknamed the pattern the “Ring of Fire,” a loose chain stretching from South America up through the western United States, across to Japan, and down through Southeast Asia. Not every volcano sits on a plate boundary, however; a smaller number, including the Hawaiian volcanoes, form instead over stationary plumes of heat rising from deep within the Earth, far from any boundary at all, which is part of why Kilauea’s activity looks so different from an explosive composite volcano thousands of miles away.

lines.html: Predicting exactly when a given volcano will erupt remains difficult, but scientists are rarely caught completely by surprise. Instruments buried near active volcanoes track subtle swelling of the ground, small earthquakes caused by moving magma, and changes in the gases escaping from vents, giving nearby communities days or weeks of warning before most major eruptions. That warning, built from decades of comparing one eruption to the next, is often the difference between a spectacular geological event and a genuine disaster, and it is why scientists continue to keep instruments running on volcanoes that have been silent for years, waiting for the small signs that come before the large ones.

lines.text: The following is adapted from “About Volcanoes,” a public-domain publication of the U.S. Geological Survey’s Volcano Hazards Program.
How a Mountain Becomes a Volcano
by the U.S. Geological Survey Volcano Hazards Program

lines.html: More than fifteen hundred volcanoes around the world are considered potentially active, not counting the thousands more hidden beneath the ocean. In the United States alone, the U.S. Geological Survey monitors upward of one hundred sixty volcanoes that have erupted in the recent geologic past or show signs that they could erupt again. Roughly five hundred volcanoes worldwide have erupted at least once within the past hundred years, and a handful, including Hawaii’s Kilauea, have been erupting almost continuously for decades at a stretch.
lines.text: More than fifteen hundred volcanoes around the world are considered potentially active, not counting the thousands more hidden beneath the ocean. Roughly five hundred volcanoes worldwide have erupted at least once within the past hundred years, and a handful, including Hawaii’s Kilauea, have been erupting almost continuously for decades at a stretch.

lines.html: A volcano begins with magma, molten rock that forms deep underground where temperatures and pressures are high enough to melt solid rock. Magma is less dense than the rock around it, so it works its way upward through cracks and weak points in the crust, sometimes pausing for years or centuries in an underground reservoir before moving again. Where it finally reaches the surface, at an opening called a vent, geologists no longer call it magma; once it breaks through, it becomes lava, along with clouds of ash, gas, and fragments of broken rock known collectively as tephra.
