directions.subject: English Language Arts
directions.title: REVISING/EDITING PART A

lines.text: The Science of Sourdough
by Devon Okafor

lines.html: (1) A jar of flour and water left on a kitchen counter looks like nothing special. (2) After a few days, bubbles rise through the mixture, and it starts to smell faintly sour. (3) This transformation produces what bakers call a sourdough starter, a small, self-sustaining ecosystem. (4) Wild yeast and naturally occurring bacteria move into the jar. (5) They begin to multiply almost immediately. (6) The yeast in a starter feeds on the natural sugars in flour, they release carbon dioxide gas as a byproduct. (7) That gas is what gets trapped in bread dough and makes it rise. (8) Bacteria living alongside the yeast produces lactic and acetic acid, which give sourdough bread its distinctive tangy flavor. (9) The exact balance of acids in a starter shapes whether a loaf tastes mild or sharply sour. (10) Some bakers keep their starters for decades, passing small portions along to friends and family. (11) Once a starter is active, a baker maintains it by discarding part of the mixture and adding fresh flour and water. (12) Bakers call this process “feeding,” and it happens roughly once a day for a starter kept at room temperature. (13) Commercial yeast, by contrast, produces the same rise and flavor in any kitchen, because it is a single cultivated strain bred for consistency rather than the wild mix of organisms a sourdough starter depends on. (14) Skipping a feeding for too long starves the yeast, and the starter developed a layer of dark liquid on top, a sign that it needs attention. lines.html: (1) A jar of flour and water left on a kitchen counter looks like nothing special. (2) After a few days, bubbles rise through the mixture, and it starts to smell faintly sour. (3) This transformation produces what bakers call a sourdough starter, a small, self-sustaining ecosystem. (4) Wild yeast and naturally occurring bacteria move into the jar. (5) They begin to multiply almost immediately. (6) The yeast in a starter feeds on the natural sugars in flour, they release carbon dioxide gas as a byproduct. (7) That gas is what gets trapped in bread dough and makes it rise. (8) Bacteria living alongside the yeast produces lactic and acetic acid, which give sourdough bread its distinctive tangy flavor. (9) The exact balance of acids in a starter shapes whether a loaf tastes mild or sharply sour. (10) Some bakers keep their starters for decades, passing small portions along to friends and family. (11) Once a starter is active, a baker maintains it by discarding part of the mixture and adding fresh flour and water. (12) Bakers call this process “feeding,” and it happens roughly once a day for a starter kept at room temperature. (13) Commercial yeast, by contrast, produces the same rise and flavor in any kitchen, because it is a single cultivated strain bred for consistency rather than the wild mix of organisms a sourdough starter depends on. (14) Skipping a feeding for too long starves the yeast, and the starter developed a layer of dark liquid on top, a sign that it needs attention. (15) Bakers refer to that liquid as “hooch,” and a small amount is harmless. (16) Not every starter behaves the same way, even when two bakers use identical flour and water. (17) A starter’s particular balance of yeast and bacteria depends on several sources of microorganisms: the flour itself, the air in the kitchen, and even the baker’s own hands. (18) A starter kept in a warm kitchen tends to rise faster than one kept in a cool basement. (19) Two starters begun on the same day, fed the same way, can taste noticeably different within a month. (20) Professional bakeries sometimes trace a single starter back for generations, treating it almost like a family heirloom. (21) A home baker who wants to try this needs only flour, water, patience, and a willingness to feed a jar of bubbling paste every day. (22) The reward, most sourdough bakers agree, is a loaf that no store-bought yeast could ever quite replicate.

(9) The exact balance of acids in a starter shapes whether a loaf tastes mild or sharply sour. (10) Some bakers keep their starters for decades, passing small portions along to friends and family. (11) Once a starter is active, a baker maintains it by discarding part of the mixture and adding fresh flour and water. (12) Bakers call this process “feeding,” and it happens roughly once a day for a starter kept at room temperature. (13) Commercial yeast, by contrast, produces the same rise and flavor in any kitchen, because it is a single cultivated strain bred for consistency rather than the wild mix of organisms a sourdough starter depends on. (14) Skipping a feeding for too long starves the yeast, and the starter developed a layer of dark liquid on top, a sign that it needs attention. (15) Bakers refer to that liquid as “hooch,” and a small amount is harmless. (16) Not every starter behaves the same way, even when two bakers use identical flour and water. (17) A starter’s particular balance of yeast and bacteria depends on several sources of microorganisms: the flour itself, the air in the kitchen, and even the baker’s own hands. (18) A starter kept in a warm kitchen tends to rise faster than one kept in a cool basement. (19) Two starters begun on the same day, fed the same way, can taste noticeably different within a month. (20) Professional bakeries sometimes trace a single starter back for generations, treating it almost like a family heirloom. (21) A home baker who wants to try this needs only flour, water, patience, and a willingness to feed a jar of bubbling paste every day. (22) The reward, most sourdough bakers agree, is a loaf that no store-bought yeast could ever quite replicate.

lines.text: Rudyard Kipling (1865-1936) was an English author born in India. "Mowgli’s Brothers" is a chapter from The Jungle Book (1894), in which a human child is adopted by a family of wolves in the Indian jungle.
lines.html: Rudyard Kipling (1865-1936) was an English author born in India. "Mowgli’s Brothers" is a chapter from The Jungle Book (1894), in which a human child is adopted by a family of wolves in the Indian jungle.

lines.text: Excerpt from "Mowgli’s Brothers"
by Rudyard Kipling

lines.html: Father Wolf listened, and below in the valley that ran down to a little river he heard the dry, angry, snarly, singsong whine of a tiger who has caught nothing and does not care if all the jungle knows it. “The fool!” said Father Wolf. “To begin a night’s work with that noise! Does he think that our buck are like his fat Waingunga bullocks?” “H’sh. It is neither bullock nor buck he hunts to-night,” said Mother Wolf. “It is Man.” The whine had changed to a sort of humming purr that seemed to come from every quarter of the compass. It was the noise that bewilders woodcutters and gypsies sleeping in the open, and makes them run sometimes into the very mouth of the tiger. “Man!” said Father Wolf, showing all his white teeth. “Faugh! Are there not enough beetles and frogs in the tanks that he must eat Man, and on our ground too!” The Law of the Jungle, which never orders anything without a reason, forbids every beast to eat Man except when he is killing to show his children how to kill, and then he must hunt outside the hunting grounds of his pack or tribe. The real reason for this is that man-killing means, sooner or later, the arrival of white men on elephants, with guns, and hundreds of brown men with gongs and rockets and torches. Then everybody in the jungle suffers. The reason the beasts give among themselves is that Man is the weakest and most defenseless of all living things, and it is unsportsmanlike to touch him. They say too--and it is true--that man-eaters become mangy, and lose their teeth.

lines.html: The purr grew louder, and ended in the full-throated “Aaarh!” of the tiger’s charge. Then there was a howl--an untigerish howl--from Shere Khan. “He has missed,” said Mother Wolf. “What is it?” Father Wolf ran out a few paces and heard Shere Khan muttering and mumbling savagely as he tumbled about in the scrub.

lines.html: “The fool has had no more sense than to jump at a woodcutter’s campfire, and has burned his feet,” said Father Wolf with a grunt. “Tabaqui is with him.” “Something is coming uphill,” said Mother Wolf, twitching one ear. “Get ready.”

lines.html: The bushes rustled a little in the thicket, and Father Wolf dropped with his haunches under him, ready for his leap. Then, if you had been watching, you would have seen the most wonderful thing in the world--the wolf checked in mid-spring. He made his bound before he saw what it was he was jumping at, and then he tried to stop himself. The result was that he shot up straight into the air for four or five feet, landing almost where he left ground. “Man!” he snapped. “A man’s cub. Look!” Directly in front of him, holding on by a low branch, stood a naked brown baby who could just walk--as soft and as dimpled a little atom as ever came to a wolf’s cave at night. He looked up into Father Wolf’s face, and laughed.

lines.html: “Is that a man’s cub?” said Mother Wolf. “I have never seen one. Bring it here.” A Wolf accustomed to moving his own cubs can, if necessary, mouth an egg without breaking it, and though Father Wolf’s jaws closed right on the child’s back not a tooth even scratched the skin as he laid it down among the cubs. “How little! How naked, and--how bold!” said Mother Wolf softly. The baby was pushing his way between the cubs to get close to the warm hide. “Ahai! He is taking his meal with the others. And so this is a man’s cub. Now, was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man’s cub among her children?”

lines.html: The moonlight was blocked out of the mouth of the cave, for Shere Khan’s great square head and shoulders were thrust into the entrance. Tabaqui, behind him, was squeaking: “My lord, my lord, it went in here!” “Shere Khan does us great honor,” said Father Wolf, but his eyes were very angry. “What does Shere Khan need?” “My quarry. A man’s cub went this way,” said Shere Khan. “Its parents have run off. Give it to me.”

lines.html: Shere Khan had jumped at a woodcutter’s campfire, as Father Wolf had said, and was furious from the pain of his burned feet. But Father Wolf knew that the mouth of the cave was too narrow for a tiger to come in by. Even where he was, Shere Khan’s shoulders and forepaws were cramped for want of room, as a man’s would be if he tried to fight in a barrel. “The Wolves are a free people,” said Father Wolf. “They take orders from the Head of the Pack, and not from any striped cattle-killer. The man’s cub is ours--to kill if we choose.” “Ye choose and ye do not choose! What talk is this of choosing? By the bull that I killed, am I to stand nosing into your dog’s den for my fair dues? It is I, Shere Khan, who speak!”

lines.html: The tiger’s roar filled the cave with thunder. Mother Wolf shook herself clear of the cubs and sprang forward, her eyes, like two green moons in the darkness, facing the blazing eyes of Shere Khan. “And it is I, Raksha [The Demon], who answers. The man’s cub is mine, Lungri--mine to me! He shall not be killed. He shall live to run with the Pack and to hunt with the Pack; and in the end, look you, hunter of little naked cubs--frog-eater--fish-killer--he shall hunt thee! Now get hence, or by the Sambhur that I killed (I eat no starved cattle), back thou goest to thy mother, burned beast of the jungle, lamer than ever thou camest into the world! Go!”

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B


Explanation: The passage separates the "real reason" involving human retaliation with guns and torches from "the reason the beasts give among themselves" about sportsmanship, showing that the jungle animals tell themselves a nobler story while the narrator reveals the more self-interested truth behind the rule.


A. Incorrect: Nothing in the passage suggests the beasts are unaware that humans are considered the weakest creature; the distinction is about which reason they choose to tell themselves, not what they know.


B. Correct: The animals embrace the flattering "sportsmanship" story instead of the blunt truth about avoiding human retaliation, which is exactly the self-serving preference the passage describes.


C. Incorrect: The two explanations are not framed as directly contradicting each other; one is simply the private truth and the other the story the animals prefer to tell.


D. Incorrect: The passage doesn't single out Shere Khan as uniquely rejecting the justifications; the contrast is between the narrator's revealed truth and what all the beasts tell themselves.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: D


Explanation: Mother Wolf springs forward and holds off a far larger, more dangerous predator purely to protect a cub that is not even her own species, showing that love and courage can outmatch brute strength in the world the passage depicts.


A. Incorrect: Mother Wolf does not submit to Shere Khan's greater size; she instead confronts him directly, which contradicts this choice.


B. Incorrect: Mother Wolf's defense of the cub does not involve abandoning the wolves' Law; if anything her stand is framed within the Law's protections.


C. Incorrect: The passage doesn't generalize about predators fearing other predators; it focuses specifically on a parent's protective courage.


D. Correct: Mother Wolf, though physically smaller than the tiger, stands her ground purely out of love for the cub, showing that courage rooted in family love can overcome a larger, stronger threat.

lines.html: Father Wolf listened, and below in the valley that ran down to a little river he heard the dry, angry, snarly, singsong whine of a tiger who has caught nothing and does not care if all the jungle knows it. “The fool!” said Father Wolf. “To begin a night’s work with that noise! Does he think that our buck are like his fat Waingunga bullocks?” “H’sh. It is neither bullock nor buck he hunts to-night,” said Mother Wolf. “It is Man.” The whine had changed to a sort of humming purr that seemed to come from every quarter of the compass. It was the noise that bewilders woodcutters and gypsies sleeping in the open, and makes them run sometimes into the very mouth of the tiger. “Man!” said Father Wolf, showing all his white teeth. “Faugh! Are there not enough beetles and frogs in the tanks that he must eat Man, and on our ground too!” The Law of the Jungle, which never orders anything without a reason, forbids every beast to eat Man except when he is killing to show his children how to kill, and then he must hunt outside the hunting grounds of his pack or tribe. The real reason for this is that man-killing means, sooner or later, the arrival of white men on elephants, with guns, and hundreds of brown men with gongs and rockets and torches. Then everybody in the jungle suffers. The reason the beasts give among themselves is that Man is the weakest and most defenseless of all living things, and it is unsportsmanlike to touch him. They say too--and it is true--that man-eaters become mangy, and lose their teeth.

lines.html: The bushes rustled a little in the thicket, and Father Wolf dropped with his haunches under him, ready for his leap. Then, if you had been watching, you would have seen the most wonderful thing in the world--the wolf checked in mid-spring. He made his bound before he saw what it was he was jumping at, and then he tried to stop himself. The result was that he shot up straight into the air for four or five feet, landing almost where he left ground. “Man!” he snapped. “A man’s cub. Look!” Directly in front of him, holding on by a low branch, stood a naked brown baby who could just walk--as soft and as dimpled a little atom as ever came to a wolf’s cave at night. He looked up into Father Wolf’s face, and laughed.

lines.html: “Is that a man’s cub?” said Mother Wolf. “I have never seen one. Bring it here.” A Wolf accustomed to moving his own cubs can, if necessary, mouth an egg without breaking it, and though Father Wolf’s jaws closed right on the child’s back not a tooth even scratched the skin as he laid it down among the cubs. “How little! How naked, and--how bold!” said Mother Wolf softly. The baby was pushing his way between the cubs to get close to the warm hide. “Ahai! He is taking his meal with the others. And so this is a man’s cub. Now, was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man’s cub among her children?”

Tabaqui, behind him, was squeaking: “My lord, my lord, it went in here!” “Shere Khan does us great honor,” said Father Wolf, but his eyes were very angry. “What does Shere Khan need?” “My quarry. A man’s cub went this way,” said Shere Khan. “Its parents have run off. Give it to me.”

But Father Wolf knew that the mouth of the cave was too narrow for a tiger to come in by. Even where he was, Shere Khan’s shoulders and forepaws were cramped for want of room, as a man’s would be if he tried to fight in a barrel. “The Wolves are a free people,” said Father Wolf. “They take orders from the Head of the Pack, and not from any striped cattle-killer. The man’s cub is ours--to kill if we choose.” “Ye choose and ye do not choose! What talk is this of choosing? By the bull that I killed, am I to stand nosing into your dog’s den for my fair dues? It is I, Shere Khan, who speak!”

lines.html: The tiger’s roar filled the cave with thunder. Mother Wolf shook herself clear of the cubs and sprang forward, her eyes, like two green moons in the darkness, facing the blazing eyes of Shere Khan. “And it is I, Raksha [The Demon], who answers. The man’s cub is mine, Lungri--mine to me! He shall not be killed. He shall live to run with the Pack and to hunt with the Pack; and in the end, look you, hunter of little naked cubs--frog-eater--fish-killer--he shall hunt thee! Now get hence, or by the Sambhur that I killed (I eat no starved cattle), back thou goest to thy mother, burned beast of the jungle, lamer than ever thou camest into the world! Go!”

lines.html: Father Wolf listened, and below in the valley that ran down to a little river he heard the dry, angry, snarly, singsong whine of a tiger who has caught nothing and does not care if all the jungle knows it. “The fool!” said Father Wolf. “To begin a night’s work with that noise! It is neither bullock nor buck he hunts to-night,” said Mother Wolf. “It is Man.” The whine had changed to a sort of humming purr that seemed to come from every quarter of the compass. It was the noise that bewilders woodcutters and gypsies sleeping in the open, and makes them run sometimes into the very mouth of the tiger. “Man!” said Father Wolf, showing all his white teeth. “Faugh! Are there not enough beetles and frogs in the tanks that he must eat Man, and on our ground too!” The Law of the Jungle, which never orders anything without a reason, forbids every beast to eat Man except when he is killing to show his children how to kill, and then he must hunt outside the hunting grounds of his pack or tribe. The real reason for this is that man-killing means, sooner or later, the arrival of white men on elephants, with guns, and hundreds of brown men with gongs and rockets and torches. Then everybody in the jungle suffers. The reason the beasts give among themselves is that Man is the weakest and most defenseless of all living things, and it is unsportsmanlike to touch him. They say too--and it is true--that man-eaters become mangy, and lose their teeth.

It is neither bullock nor buck he hunts to-night,” said Mother Wolf. “It is Man.” The whine had changed to a sort of humming purr that seemed to come from every quarter of the compass. It was the noise that bewilders woodcutters and gypsies sleeping in the open, and makes them run sometimes into the very mouth of the tiger. “Man!” said Father Wolf, showing all his white teeth. “Faugh! The real reason for this is that man-killing means, sooner or later, the arrival of white men on elephants, with guns, and hundreds of brown men with gongs and rockets and torches. They say too--and it is true--that man-eaters become mangy, and lose their teeth.

lines.html: The bushes rustled a little in the thicket, and Father Wolf dropped with his haunches under him, ready for his leap. Then, if you had been watching, you would have seen the most wonderful thing in the world--the wolf checked in mid-spring. He made his bound before he saw what it was he was jumping at, and then he tried to stop himself. The result was that he shot up straight into the air for four or five feet, landing almost where he left ground. “Man!” he snapped. “A man’s cub. Look!” Directly in front of him, holding on by a low branch, stood a naked brown baby who could just walk--as soft and as dimpled a little atom as ever came to a wolf’s cave at night. He looked up into Father Wolf’s face, and laughed.

lines.html: “Is that a man’s cub?” said Mother Wolf. “I have never seen one. Bring it here.” A Wolf accustomed to moving his own cubs can, if necessary, mouth an egg without breaking it, and though Father Wolf’s jaws closed right on the child’s back not a tooth even scratched the skin as he laid it down among the cubs. “How little! How naked, and--how bold!” said Mother Wolf softly. The baby was pushing his way between the cubs to get close to the warm hide. “Ahai! He is taking his meal with the others. And so this is a man’s cub. Now, was there ever a wolf that could boast of a man’s cub among her children?”

lines.html: The moonlight was blocked out of the mouth of the cave, for Shere Khan’s great square head and shoulders were thrust into the entrance. Tabaqui, behind him, was squeaking: “My lord, my lord, it went in here!” “Shere Khan does us great honor,” said Father Wolf, but his eyes were very angry. “What does Shere Khan need?” “My quarry. A man’s cub went this way,” said Shere Khan. “Its parents have run off. Give it to me.”

lines.html: Shere Khan had jumped at a woodcutter’s campfire, as Father Wolf had said, and was furious from the pain of his burned feet. But Father Wolf knew that the mouth of the cave was too narrow for a tiger to come in by. Even where he was, Shere Khan’s shoulders and forepaws were cramped for want of room, as a man’s would be if he tried to fight in a barrel. “The Wolves are a free people,” said Father Wolf. “They take orders from the Head of the Pack, and not from any striped cattle-killer. The man’s cub is ours--to kill if we choose.” “Ye choose and ye do not choose! What talk is this of choosing? By the bull that I killed, am I to stand nosing into your dog’s den for my fair dues? It is I, Shere Khan, who speak!”

lines.html: The tiger’s roar filled the cave with thunder. Mother Wolf shook herself clear of the cubs and sprang forward, her eyes, like two green moons in the darkness, facing the blazing eyes of Shere Khan. “And it is I, Raksha [The Demon], who answers. The man’s cub is mine, Lungri--mine to me! He shall not be killed. He shall live to run with the Pack and to hunt with the Pack; and in the end, look you, hunter of little naked cubs--frog-eater--fish-killer--he shall hunt thee! Now get hence, or by the Sambhur that I killed (I eat no starved cattle), back thou goest to thy mother, burned beast of the jungle, lamer than ever thou camest into the world! Go!”

lines.html: Eleanor Voss writes about the history of architecture and engineering for a regional heritage magazine. The following is adapted from her article on an early concert hall renovation.

lines.text: Excerpt from "The Hall That Learned to Listen"
by Eleanor Voss

lines.html: In 1886 the newly built Whitcombe Assembly Hall opened in a resort town tucked into the mountains, meant to give summer visitors an elegant place to hear touring orchestras during the warm months when the rest of the season's entertainment moved indoors. Its architects had studied the great concert halls of Europe and copied their proportions closely: a long rectangular room, a high coffered ceiling, and rows of hard wooden benches facing a modest stage framed by carved pillars. On opening night the orchestra played to a full house, and for the first several minutes the audience seemed delighted simply to be there, in a room built for exactly this purpose. But by the second movement, listeners in the rear third of the hall were leaning forward, straining to separate one instrument from another. The sound that reached them arrived blurred, as though several performances were overlapping in the air above their heads, each note still ringing when the next one began.
lines.text: In 1886 the newly built Whitcombe Assembly Hall opened in a resort town tucked into the mountains, meant to give summer visitors an elegant place to hear touring orchestras during the warm months when the rest of the season's entertainment moved indoors. Its architects had studied the great concert halls of Europe and copied their proportions closely: a long rectangular room, a high coffered ceiling, and rows of hard wooden benches facing a modest stage framed by carved pillars. On opening night the orchestra played to a full house, and for the first several minutes the audience seemed delighted simply to be there, in a room built for exactly this purpose. But by the second movement, listeners in the rear third of the hall were leaning forward, straining to separate one instrument from another. The sound that reached them arrived blurred, as though several performances were overlapping in the air above their heads, each note still ringing when the next one began.

lines.html: The hall's manager, uncertain what had gone wrong, called in carpenters and upholsterers rather than scientists, since no formal science of architectural acoustics yet existed to consult. Reverberation, the way sound persists and piles up as it bounces repeatedly off hard, flat surfaces, would not be measured and explained mathematically for another decade. What the Whitcombe's builders had instead was patience and a willingness to guess, test, and guess again. Over one off-season they hung heavy curtains along the side walls, laid a thick carpet runner down the center aisle, and replaced a stretch of the rear wall's smooth plaster with a shallow, ridged wooden panel meant to scatter sound in many directions rather than throw it directly back toward the stage in a single hard reflection.

What the Whitcombe's builders had instead was patience and a willingness to guess, test, and guess again. Over one off-season they hung heavy curtains along the side walls, laid a thick carpet runner down the center aisle, and replaced a stretch of the rear wall's smooth plaster with a shallow, ridged wooden panel meant to scatter sound in many directions rather than throw it directly back toward the stage in a single hard reflection.

lines.html: To judge whether the changes had worked, the hall's resident engineer returned each evening for two weeks with a stopwatch and an assistant stationed at the stage with a small hand bell. From five fixed seats spread around the hall, she timed how long a single sharp ring remained faintly audible before it dropped below hearing, a rough but workable stand-in for what acousticians would later call reverberation time. Her nightly measurements, recorded seat by seat, are collected in the table accompanying this article. They show clear improvement almost everywhere, though not evenly: the orchestra floor, close to the stage and already surrounded by absorbent bench cushions, had never lingered long to begin with, while the rear balcony and the seats tucked beneath its overhang stayed noticeably livelier than the rest of the hall even after every fix on the list had been tried.

They show clear improvement almost everywhere, though not evenly: the orchestra floor, close to the stage and already surrounded by absorbent bench cushions, had never lingered long to begin with, while the rear balcony and the seats tucked beneath its overhang stayed noticeably livelier than the rest of the hall even after every fix on the list had been tried.

lines.html: The pattern in the numbers matched what the ushers had been hearing all along from patrons on their way out, and it pointed the renovation crew toward the one area still unaddressed: the curved plaster ceiling above the rear overhang, which had been throwing sound back down onto the seats below almost undiminished, adding an extra half second or more of lingering echo exactly where listeners could least afford it. A final round of work hung absorbent panels along that curve, and by the hall's third season, letters from subscribers no longer mentioned muddiness at all, only the ordinary complaints of ticket prices and drafty doors.

lines.html: None of this required the mathematics that would later let architects predict a room's reverberation time before a single wall was built, using nothing more than a floor plan and a list of the materials to be used. It required only careful listening, a willingness to test one change at a time instead of several at once, and a record kept honestly enough to show which fixes had actually worked and which had simply felt like they should. Sabine's formula, when it finally arrived, would let architects design a concert hall's proportions and materials on paper and know in advance roughly how long a handclap would ring in the finished room.

Sabine's formula, when it finally arrived, would let architects design a concert hall's proportions and materials on paper and know in advance roughly how long a handclap would ring in the finished room.

lines.html: What is striking, looking back at the Whitcombe's log book today, is how closely its conclusions anticipated that later science. Enclosed, overhung spaces trap sound longer than open ones; soft, irregular surfaces calm a room that hard, flat ones stir into confusion. The hall's engineer had no equation for any of this. She had only a stopwatch, a bell, and the discipline to write down what she actually heard rather than what the architects had promised her she would hear.

lines.text: Eleanor Voss writes about the history of architecture and engineering for a regional heritage magazine. The following is adapted from her article on an early concert hall renovation.
lines.html: Eleanor Voss writes about the history of architecture and engineering for a regional heritage magazine. The following is adapted from her article on an early concert hall renovation.

lines.text: Excerpt from "The Hall That Learned to Listen"
by Eleanor Voss

lines.html: In 1886 the newly built Whitcombe Assembly Hall opened in a resort town tucked into the mountains, meant to give summer visitors an elegant place to hear touring orchestras during the warm months when the rest of the season's entertainment moved indoors. Its architects had studied the great concert halls of Europe and copied their proportions closely: a long rectangular room, a high coffered ceiling, and rows of hard wooden benches facing a modest stage framed by carved pillars. On opening night the orchestra played to a full house, and for the first several minutes the audience seemed delighted simply to be there, in a room built for exactly this purpose. But by the second movement, listeners in the rear third of the hall were leaning forward, straining to separate one instrument from another. The sound that reached them arrived blurred, as though several performances were overlapping in the air above their heads, each note still ringing when the next one began.

lines.text: Charles Darwin (1809-1882) was an English naturalist. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) is his journal from a five-year scientific survey expedition aboard the HMS Beagle.
lines.html: Charles Darwin (1809-1882) was an English naturalist. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) is his journal from a five-year scientific survey expedition aboard the HMS Beagle.

lines.text: Excerpt from "Excerpt from "The Voyage of the Beagle""
lines.html: Excerpt from "Excerpt from "The Voyage of the Beagle""

lines.text: by Charles Darwin
lines.html: by Charles Darwin

AFTER having been twice driven back by heavy southwestern gales, Her Majesty's ship Beagle, a ten-gun brig under the command of Captain Fitz Roy, R. N., sailed from Devonport on the 27th of December, 1831, bound on a long surveying voyage around the world. On the 6th of January we reached Teneriffe, but were prevented landing by fears of our bringing the cholera; the next morning we saw the sun rise behind the rugged outline of the Grand Canary island and suddenly illuminate the Peak of Teneriffe, whilst the lower parts were veiled in fleecy clouds. On the 16th of January, 1832, we anchored at Porto Praya, in St. Jago, the chief island of the Cape de Verd archipelago.

N., sailed from Devonport on the 27th of December, 1831, bound on a long surveying voyage around the world. On the 6th of January we reached Teneriffe, but were prevented landing by fears of our bringing the cholera; the next morning we saw the sun rise behind the rugged outline of the Grand Canary island and suddenly illuminate the Peak of Teneriffe, whilst the lower parts were veiled in fleecy clouds. On the 16th of January, 1832, we anchored at Porto Praya, in St. Jago, the chief island of the Cape de Verd archipelago.

lines.html: The neighbourhood of Porto Praya, viewed from the sea, wears a desolate aspect. The volcanic fires of a past age, and the scorching heat of a tropical sun, have in most places rendered the soil unfit for vegetation. The country rises in successive steps of table-land, interspersed with some truncate conical hills, and the horizon is bounded by an irregular chain of more lofty mountains. The scene, as beheld through the hazy atmosphere of this climate, is one of great interest; if, indeed, a person, fresh from sea, and who has just walked, for the first time, in a grove of cocoa-nut trees, can be a judge of anything but his own happiness. The island would generally be considered as very uninteresting, but to anyone accustomed only to an English landscape, the novel aspect of an utterly sterile land possesses a grandeur which more vegetation might spoil.

lines.html: A single green leaf can scarcely be discovered over wide tracts of the lava plains; yet flocks of goats, together with a few cows, contrive to exist. It rains very seldom, but during a short portion of the year heavy torrents fall, and immediately afterwards a light vegetation springs out of every crevice. This soon withers; and upon such naturally formed hay the animals live. It had not now rained for an entire year. When the island was discovered, the immediate neighbourhood of Porto Praya was clothed with trees, the reckless destruction of which has caused here, as at St. Helena, and at some of the Canary islands, almost entire sterility. The broad, flat-bottomed valleys, many of which serve during a few days only in the season as water-courses, are clothed with thickets of leafless bushes. Few living creatures inhabit these valleys. The commonest bird is a kingfisher (Dacelo Iagoensis), which tamely sits on the branches of the castor-oil plant, and thence darts on grasshoppers and lizards. It is brightly coloured, but not so beautiful as the European species: in its flight, manners, and place of habitation, which is generally in the driest valley, there is also a wide difference.

lines.html: One day, two of the officers and myself rode to Ribeira Grande, a village a few miles eastward of Porto Praya. Until we reached the valley of St. Martin, the country presented its usual dull brown appearance; but here, a very small rill of water produces a most refreshing margin of luxuriant vegetation. In the course of an hour we arrived at Ribeira Grande, and were surprised at the sight of a large ruined fort and cathedral. This little town, before its harbour was filled up, was the principal place in the island: it now presents a melancholy, but very picturesque appearance. Having procured a local guide and an interpreter who had served in the Peninsular war, we visited a collection of buildings, of which an ancient church formed the principal part. It is here the governors and captain-generals of the islands have been buried. Some of the tombstones recorded dates of the sixteenth century.

lines.html: The geology of this island is the most interesting part of its natural history. On entering the harbour, a perfectly horizontal white band, in the face of the sea cliff, may be seen running for some miles along the coast, and at the height of about forty-five feet above the water. Upon examination this white stratum is found to consist of calcareous matter with numerous shells embedded, most or all of which now exist on the neighbouring coast. It rests on ancient volcanic rocks, and has been covered by a stream of basalt, which must have entered the sea when the white shelly bed was lying at the bottom. It is interesting to trace the changes produced by the heat of the overlying lava on this friable mass, which in parts has been converted into a crystalline limestone, and in other parts into a compact spotted stone.

lines.html: The beds of lava rise in successive gently-sloping plains toward the interior, whence the deluges of melted stone have originally proceeded. Within historical times, no signs of volcanic activity have, I believe, been manifested in any part of St. Jago. Even the form of a crater can but rarely be discovered on the summits of the many red cindery hills; yet the more recent streams can be distinguished on the coast, forming lines of cliffs of less height, but stretching out in advance of those belonging to an older series: the height of the cliffs thus affording a rude measure of the age of the streams.

lines.text: by Charles Darwin
lines.html: by Charles Darwin

AFTER having been twice driven back by heavy southwestern gales, Her Majesty's ship Beagle, a ten-gun brig under the command of Captain Fitz Roy, R. N., sailed from Devonport on the 27th of December, 1831, bound on a long surveying voyage around the world. On the 6th of January we reached Teneriffe, but were prevented landing by fears of our bringing the cholera; the next morning we saw the sun rise behind the rugged outline of the Grand Canary island and suddenly illuminate the Peak of Teneriffe, whilst the lower parts were veiled in fleecy clouds. On the 16th of January, 1832, we anchored at Porto Praya, in St. Jago, the chief island of the Cape de Verd archipelago.

On the 6th of January we reached Teneriffe, but were prevented landing by fears of our bringing the cholera; the next morning we saw the sun rise behind the rugged outline of the Grand Canary island and suddenly illuminate the Peak of Teneriffe, whilst the lower parts were veiled in fleecy clouds. On the 16th of January, 1832, we anchored at Porto Praya, in St. Jago, the chief island of the Cape de Verd archipelago.

lines.html: The neighbourhood of Porto Praya, viewed from the sea, wears a desolate aspect. The volcanic fires of a past age, and the scorching heat of a tropical sun, have in most places rendered the soil unfit for vegetation. The country rises in successive steps of table-land, interspersed with some truncate conical hills, and the horizon is bounded by an irregular chain of more lofty mountains. The scene, as beheld through the hazy atmosphere of this climate, is one of great interest; if, indeed, a person, fresh from sea, and who has just walked, for the first time, in a grove of cocoa-nut trees, can be a judge of anything but his own happiness. The island would generally be considered as very uninteresting, but to anyone accustomed only to an English landscape, the novel aspect of an utterly sterile land possesses a grandeur which more vegetation might spoil.

lines.html: A single green leaf can scarcely be discovered over wide tracts of the lava plains; yet flocks of goats, together with a few cows, contrive to exist. It rains very seldom, but during a short portion of the year heavy torrents fall, and immediately afterwards a light vegetation springs out of every crevice. This soon withers; and upon such naturally formed hay the animals live. It had not now rained for an entire year. When the island was discovered, the immediate neighbourhood of Porto Praya was clothed with trees, the reckless destruction of which has caused here, as at St. Helena, and at some of the Canary islands, almost entire sterility. The broad, flat-bottomed valleys, many of which serve during a few days only in the season as water-courses, are clothed with thickets of leafless bushes. Few living creatures inhabit these valleys. The commonest bird is a kingfisher (Dacelo Iagoensis), which tamely sits on the branches of the castor-oil plant, and thence darts on grasshoppers and lizards. It is brightly coloured, but not so beautiful as the European species: in its flight, manners, and place of habitation, which is generally in the driest valley, there is also a wide difference.

lines.html: One day, two of the officers and myself rode to Ribeira Grande, a village a few miles eastward of Porto Praya. Until we reached the valley of St. Martin, the country presented its usual dull brown appearance; but here, a very small rill of water produces a most refreshing margin of luxuriant vegetation. In the course of an hour we arrived at Ribeira Grande, and were surprised at the sight of a large ruined fort and cathedral. This little town, before its harbour was filled up, was the principal place in the island: it now presents a melancholy, but very picturesque appearance. Having procured a local guide and an interpreter who had served in the Peninsular war, we visited a collection of buildings, of which an ancient church formed the principal part. It is here the governors and captain-generals of the islands have been buried. Some of the tombstones recorded dates of the sixteenth century.

lines.html: The geology of this island is the most interesting part of its natural history. On entering the harbour, a perfectly horizontal white band, in the face of the sea cliff, may be seen running for some miles along the coast, and at the height of about forty-five feet above the water. Upon examination this white stratum is found to consist of calcareous matter with numerous shells embedded, most or all of which now exist on the neighbouring coast. It rests on ancient volcanic rocks, and has been covered by a stream of basalt, which must have entered the sea when the white shelly bed was lying at the bottom. It is interesting to trace the changes produced by the heat of the overlying lava on this friable mass, which in parts has been converted into a crystalline limestone, and in other parts into a compact spotted stone.

lines.html: The beds of lava rise in successive gently-sloping plains toward the interior, whence the deluges of melted stone have originally proceeded. Within historical times, no signs of volcanic activity have, I believe, been manifested in any part of St. Jago. Even the form of a crater can but rarely be discovered on the summits of the many red cindery hills; yet the more recent streams can be distinguished on the coast, forming lines of cliffs of less height, but stretching out in advance of those belonging to an older series: the height of the cliffs thus affording a rude measure of the age of the streams.

The country rises in successive steps of table-land, interspersed with some truncate conical hills, and the horizon is bounded by an irregular chain of more lofty mountains. In the course of an hour we arrived at Ribeira Grande, and were surprised at the sight of a large ruined fort and cathedral. This little town, before its harbour was filled up, was the principal place in the island: it now presents a melancholy, but very picturesque appearance. Having procured a local guide and an interpreter who had served in the Peninsular war, we visited a collection of buildings, of which an ancient church formed the principal part. It is here the governors and captain-generals of the islands have been buried. Some of the tombstones recorded dates of the sixteenth century.

lines.html: The geology of this island is the most interesting part of its natural history. On entering the harbour, a perfectly horizontal white band, in the face of the sea cliff, may be seen running for some miles along the coast, and at the height of about forty-five feet above the water. Upon examination this white stratum is found to consist of calcareous matter with numerous shells embedded, most or all of which now exist on the neighbouring coast. It rests on ancient volcanic rocks, and has been covered by a stream of basalt, which must have entered the sea when the white shelly bed was lying at the bottom. It is interesting to trace the changes produced by the heat of the overlying lava on this friable mass, which in parts has been converted into a crystalline limestone, and in other parts into a compact spotted stone.

lines.html: The beds of lava rise in successive gently-sloping plains toward the interior, whence the deluges of melted stone have originally proceeded. Within historical times, no signs of volcanic activity have, I believe, been manifested in any part of St. Jago. Even the form of a crater can but rarely be discovered on the summits of the many red cindery hills; yet the more recent streams can be distinguished on the coast, forming lines of cliffs of less height, but stretching out in advance of those belonging to an older series: the height of the cliffs thus affording a rude measure of the age of the streams.

lines.html: Excerpt from "Excerpt from "The Voyage of the Beagle""

lines.text: by Charles Darwin
lines.html: by Charles Darwin

AFTER having been twice driven back by heavy southwestern gales, Her Majesty's ship Beagle, a ten-gun brig under the command of Captain Fitz Roy, R. N., sailed from Devonport on the 27th of December, 1831, bound on a long surveying voyage around the world. On the 6th of January we reached Teneriffe, but were prevented landing by fears of our bringing the cholera; the next morning we saw the sun rise behind the rugged outline of the Grand Canary island and suddenly illuminate the Peak of Teneriffe, whilst the lower parts were veiled in fleecy clouds. On the 16th of January, 1832, we anchored at Porto Praya, in St. Jago, the chief island of the Cape de Verd archipelago.

On the 16th of January, 1832, we anchored at Porto Praya, in St. Jago, the chief island of the Cape de Verd archipelago.

lines.html: The neighbourhood of Porto Praya, viewed from the sea, wears a desolate aspect. The volcanic fires of a past age, and the scorching heat of a tropical sun, have in most places rendered the soil unfit for vegetation. The country rises in successive steps of table-land, interspersed with some truncate conical hills, and the horizon is bounded by an irregular chain of more lofty mountains. The scene, as beheld through the hazy atmosphere of this climate, is one of great interest; if, indeed, a person, fresh from sea, and who has just walked, for the first time, in a grove of cocoa-nut trees, can be a judge of anything but his own happiness. The island would generally be considered as very uninteresting, but to anyone accustomed only to an English landscape, the novel aspect of an utterly sterile land possesses a grandeur which more vegetation might spoil.

lines.html: A single green leaf can scarcely be discovered over wide tracts of the lava plains; yet flocks of goats, together with a few cows, contrive to exist. It rains very seldom, but during a short portion of the year heavy torrents fall, and immediately afterwards a light vegetation springs out of every crevice. This soon withers; and upon such naturally formed hay the animals live. It had not now rained for an entire year. When the island was discovered, the immediate neighbourhood of Porto Praya was clothed with trees, the reckless destruction of which has caused here, as at St. Helena, and at some of the Canary islands, almost entire sterility. The broad, flat-bottomed valleys, many of which serve during a few days only in the season as water-courses, are clothed with thickets of leafless bushes. Few living creatures inhabit these valleys. The commonest bird is a kingfisher (Dacelo Iagoensis), which tamely sits on the branches of the castor-oil plant, and thence darts on grasshoppers and lizards. It is brightly coloured, but not so beautiful as the European species: in its flight, manners, and place of habitation, which is generally in the driest valley, there is also a wide difference.

questions.explanation:
Correct Answer: B


Explanation: The final stanza pairs the speaker's admission that the woods are 'lovely, dark and deep' with the repeated line about miles still to go, so the repetition underscores that obligation ultimately outweighs the wish to stay.


A. Incorrect: Nothing in the stanza suggests the speaker gives in to exhaustion or falls asleep.


B. Correct: The repeated line pairs the admission that the woods are lovely with the unfinished duty of "miles to go," stressing how obligation weighs against the wish to stay.


C. Incorrect: The horse's restlessness is described earlier in the poem, not through this repeated final line.


D. Incorrect: While the repetition does complete the rhyme, the content of the repeated line points to thematic emphasis rather than mere rhyme-filling.

passage.title: Excerpt from "The Grip That Shouldn’t Work"

lines.text: Simone Nakamura is a science writer who covers biomechanics and materials science. The following is adapted from her article on how geckos climb smooth vertical surfaces.
lines.html: Simone Nakamura is a science writer who covers biomechanics and materials science. The following is adapted from her article on how geckos climb smooth vertical surfaces.

lines.text: Excerpt from "The Grip That Shouldn’t Work"
lines.html: Excerpt from "The Grip That Shouldn’t Work"

lines.text: by Simone Nakamura
lines.html: by Simone Nakamura

A gecko can sprint up a pane of window glass, cross onto the ceiling, and hang there by a single toe, upside down, without ever slowing to find a grip. For a long time this seemed to demand some kind of trick: a sticky secretion, perhaps, left behind wherever the foot touched, or thousands of microscopic suction cups pressed flat against the glass. Both explanations turn out to be wrong. Wipe a gecko's foot clean and press it to glass and it grips exactly as well as before, which rules out any residue. Place it in a sealed chamber with the air pumped out, removing any possibility of suction, and the grip holds just as strongly. The real explanation is stranger than either guess, since it depends on a force so weak that a single instance of it could not hold up a grain of sand, let alone a lizard.
lines.text: A gecko can sprint up a pane of window glass, cross onto the ceiling, and hang there by a single toe, upside down, without ever slowing to find a grip. For a long time this seemed to demand some kind of trick: a sticky secretion, perhaps, left behind wherever the foot touched, or thousands of microscopic suction cups pressed flat against the glass. Both explanations turn out to be wrong. Wipe a gecko's foot clean and press it to glass and it grips exactly as well as before, which rules out any residue. Place it in a sealed chamber with the air pumped out, removing any possibility of suction, and the grip holds just as strongly. The real explanation is stranger than either guess, since it depends on a force so weak that a single instance of it could not hold up a grain of sand, let alone a lizard.

lines.html: The gecko's foot is covered in ridges of hair-like structures called setae, each thinner than a human hair and packed so densely that a single toe carries roughly half a million of them. Under a microscope, every seta splits at its tip into hundreds of even finer branches, called spatulae, each one flattened like a tiny paddle only a few hundred nanometers across. It is at this scale, far below anything the unaided eye could resolve, that the actual grip takes place. When a spatula presses close enough to a surface, the electrons orbiting its atoms and the electrons in the surface's atoms begin to tug at one another, forming a weak attraction known as a van der Waals force. No glue, no moisture, and no muscular clamping are involved at all; the same attraction exists, faintly, between almost any two surfaces brought close enough together, whether or not either one is alive.
lines.text: The gecko's foot is covered in ridges of hair-like structures called setae, each thinner than a human hair and packed so densely that a single toe carries roughly half a million of them. Under a microscope, every seta splits at its tip into hundreds of even finer branches, called spatulae, each one flattened like a tiny paddle only a few hundred nanometers across. It is at this scale, far below anything the unaided eye could resolve, that the actual grip takes place. When a spatula presses close enough to a surface, the electrons orbiting its atoms and the electrons in the surface's atoms begin to tug at one another, forming a weak attraction known as a van der Waals force. No glue, no moisture, and no muscular clamping are involved at all; the same attraction exists, faintly, between almost any two surfaces brought close enough together, whether or not either one is alive.

lines.html: A single van der Waals attraction is almost nothing, far too faint to notice in ordinary life. What makes the gecko's grip strong is sheer number. Multiplied across hundreds of millions of spatulae spread over all four feet, these countless weak pulls add up to an adhesive force many times the gecko's own body weight, more than enough to let it hang from a single toe. Researchers who have measured this directly, by attaching tiny force sensors to a gecko's foot as it clings to a glass plate and gently pulling until the grip releases, have recorded forces strong enough that a sheet of spatulae the size of a human hand, if such a thing existed, could theoretically support the weight of an adult person.
lines.text: A single van der Waals attraction is almost nothing, far too faint to notice in ordinary life. What makes the gecko's grip strong is sheer number. Multiplied across hundreds of millions of spatulae spread over all four feet, these countless weak pulls add up to an adhesive force many times the gecko's own body weight, more than enough to let it hang from a single toe. Researchers who have measured this directly, by attaching tiny force sensors to a gecko's foot as it clings to a glass plate and gently pulling until the grip releases, have recorded forces strong enough that a sheet of spatulae the size of a human hand, if such a thing existed, could theoretically support the weight of an adult person.

lines.html: The gecko does not simply mash its foot against a surface and stay stuck forever, which would make climbing impossible rather than easy. Instead it engages and releases its grip with each step, angling its toes to bring the spatulae into close contact on the way down and peeling them away, a fraction of a degree at a time, on the way up. That peeling angle turns out to matter enormously: press a seta straight down against a surface and it grips fiercely, but tilt it back past a certain point, roughly thirty degrees in most studies, and the same structure releases almost instantly, with barely any effort at all. A gecko crossing a ceiling is, in effect, constantly attaching and detaching millions of microscopic hooks in a single fluid motion, fast enough that the whole process looks, to a human eye, like nothing more than an ordinary walk.

That peeling angle turns out to matter enormously: press a seta straight down against a surface and it grips fiercely, but tilt it back past a certain point, roughly thirty degrees in most studies, and the same structure releases almost instantly, with barely any effort at all. A gecko crossing a ceiling is, in effect, constantly attaching and detaching millions of microscopic hooks in a single fluid motion, fast enough that the whole process looks, to a human eye, like nothing more than an ordinary walk.

lines.html: Not every surface cooperates equally well. Setae grip smooth glass or polished stone with ease, since the spatulae can settle into close, uninterrupted contact across a wide area. On loosely packed sand or fine dust, by contrast, even a gecko's remarkable foot struggles, because the surface itself keeps shifting and breaking the contact before the van der Waals force has a chance to build. This limitation offers a kind of confirmation of the whole explanation: a sticky secretion would work about as well on either surface, and a suction cup would fail on both, but a force that depends on extremely close, stable contact would behave exactly as the gecko's grip actually does, strong on glass and weak on sand.

lines.html: Understanding this mechanism has done more than settle an old question about lizards. Engineers have already built experimental adhesive tape and robot footpads modeled on the same branching, angle-dependent structure, aiming for a grip that holds firmly under load yet releases cleanly and leaves no residue behind, unlike ordinary tape or glue. None of these materials yet matches what evolution produced in a gecko's toe, but each attempt starts from the same discovery: a force too weak to matter on its own can become one of the strongest grips in nature, once it is divided finely enough and multiplied often enough.

Explanation: Paragraph 1 sets up the mystery by calling the true cause "stranger than either guess," and paragraphs 2 and 3 reveal that a single van der Waals attraction is almost nothing on its own but becomes powerful once it is repeated across hundreds of millions of spatulae, which is exactly the surprising pattern the earlier phrase prepares readers to expect.


A. Correct: The individually faint van der Waals attraction becomes powerful once multiplied across hundreds of millions of spatulae, matching the "stranger than either guess" setup.


B. Incorrect: The passage explicitly rules out a bonding substance as the explanation.

D. Incorrect: The passage doesn't describe muscles operating tiny suction cups; that is one of the incorrect guesses being ruled out.

lines.text: by Simone Nakamura
lines.html: by Simone Nakamura

A gecko can sprint up a pane of window glass, cross onto the ceiling, and hang there by a single toe, upside down, without ever slowing to find a grip. For a long time this seemed to demand some kind of trick: a sticky secretion, perhaps, left behind wherever the foot touched, or thousands of microscopic suction cups pressed flat against the glass. Both explanations turn out to be wrong. Wipe a gecko's foot clean and press it to glass and it grips exactly as well as before, which rules out any residue. Place it in a sealed chamber with the air pumped out, removing any possibility of suction, and the grip holds just as strongly. The real explanation is stranger than either guess, since it depends on a force so weak that a single instance of it could not hold up a grain of sand, let alone a lizard.

For a long time this seemed to demand some kind of trick: a sticky secretion, perhaps, left behind wherever the foot touched, or thousands of microscopic suction cups pressed flat against the glass. Both explanations turn out to be wrong. Wipe a gecko's foot clean and press it to glass and it grips exactly as well as before, which rules out any residue. Place it in a sealed chamber with the air pumped out, removing any possibility of suction, and the grip holds just as strongly. The real explanation is stranger than either guess, since it depends on a force so weak that a single instance of it could not hold up a grain of sand, let alone a lizard.

lines.html: The gecko's foot is covered in ridges of hair-like structures called setae, each thinner than a human hair and packed so densely that a single toe carries roughly half a million of them. Under a microscope, every seta splits at its tip into hundreds of even finer branches, called spatulae, each one flattened like a tiny paddle only a few hundred nanometers across. It is at this scale, far below anything the unaided eye could resolve, that the actual grip takes place. When a spatula presses close enough to a surface, the electrons orbiting its atoms and the electrons in the surface's atoms begin to tug at one another, forming a weak attraction known as a van der Waals force. No glue, no moisture, and no muscular clamping are involved at all; the same attraction exists, faintly, between almost any two surfaces brought close enough together, whether or not either one is alive.

It is at this scale, far below anything the unaided eye could resolve, that the actual grip takes place. When a spatula presses close enough to a surface, the electrons orbiting its atoms and the electrons in the surface's atoms begin to tug at one another, forming a weak attraction known as a van der Waals force. No glue, no moisture, and no muscular clamping are involved at all; the same attraction exists, faintly, between almost any two surfaces brought close enough together, whether or not either one is alive.

lines.html: A single van der Waals attraction is almost nothing, far too faint to notice in ordinary life. What makes the gecko's grip strong is sheer number. Multiplied across hundreds of millions of spatulae spread over all four feet, these countless weak pulls add up to an adhesive force many times the gecko's own body weight, more than enough to let it hang from a single toe. Researchers who have measured this directly, by attaching tiny force sensors to a gecko's foot as it clings to a glass plate and gently pulling until the grip releases, have recorded forces strong enough that a sheet of spatulae the size of a human hand, if such a thing existed, could theoretically support the weight of an adult person.

Multiplied across hundreds of millions of spatulae spread over all four feet, these countless weak pulls add up to an adhesive force many times the gecko's own body weight, more than enough to let it hang from a single toe. Researchers who have measured this directly, by attaching tiny force sensors to a gecko's foot as it clings to a glass plate and gently pulling until the grip releases, have recorded forces strong enough that a sheet of spatulae the size of a human hand, if such a thing existed, could theoretically support the weight of an adult person.

lines.html: The gecko does not simply mash its foot against a surface and stay stuck forever, which would make climbing impossible rather than easy. Instead it engages and releases its grip with each step, angling its toes to bring the spatulae into close contact on the way down and peeling them away, a fraction of a degree at a time, on the way up. That peeling angle turns out to matter enormously: press a seta straight down against a surface and it grips fiercely, but tilt it back past a certain point, roughly thirty degrees in most studies, and the same structure releases almost instantly, with barely any effort at all. A gecko crossing a ceiling is, in effect, constantly attaching and detaching millions of microscopic hooks in a single fluid motion, fast enough that the whole process looks, to a human eye, like nothing more than an ordinary walk.

lines.html: Not every surface cooperates equally well. Setae grip smooth glass or polished stone with ease, since the spatulae can settle into close, uninterrupted contact across a wide area. On loosely packed sand or fine dust, by contrast, even a gecko's remarkable foot struggles, because the surface itself keeps shifting and breaking the contact before the van der Waals force has a chance to build. This limitation offers a kind of confirmation of the whole explanation: a sticky secretion would work about as well on either surface, and a suction cup would fail on both, but a force that depends on extremely close, stable contact would behave exactly as the gecko's grip actually does, strong on glass and weak on sand.

lines.html: Understanding this mechanism has done more than settle an old question about lizards. Engineers have already built experimental adhesive tape and robot footpads modeled on the same branching, angle-dependent structure, aiming for a grip that holds firmly under load yet releases cleanly and leaves no residue behind, unlike ordinary tape or glue. None of these materials yet matches what evolution produced in a gecko's toe, but each attempt starts from the same discovery: a force too weak to matter on its own can become one of the strongest grips in nature, once it is divided finely enough and multiplied often enough.

This limitation offers a kind of confirmation of the whole explanation: a sticky secretion would work about as well on either surface, and a suction cup would fail on both, but a force that depends on extremely close, stable contact would behave exactly as the gecko's grip actually does, strong on glass and weak on sand.

lines.html: Understanding this mechanism has done more than settle an old question about lizards. Engineers have already built experimental adhesive tape and robot footpads modeled on the same branching, angle-dependent structure, aiming for a grip that holds firmly under load yet releases cleanly and leaves no residue behind, unlike ordinary tape or glue. None of these materials yet matches what evolution produced in a gecko's toe, but each attempt starts from the same discovery: a force too weak to matter on its own can become one of the strongest grips in nature, once it is divided finely enough and multiplied often enough.

lines.text: by Simone Nakamura
lines.html: by Simone Nakamura

A gecko can sprint up a pane of window glass, cross onto the ceiling, and hang there by a single toe, upside down, without ever slowing to find a grip. For a long time this seemed to demand some kind of trick: a sticky secretion, perhaps, left behind wherever the foot touched, or thousands of microscopic suction cups pressed flat against the glass. Both explanations turn out to be wrong. Wipe a gecko's foot clean and press it to glass and it grips exactly as well as before, which rules out any residue. Place it in a sealed chamber with the air pumped out, removing any possibility of suction, and the grip holds just as strongly. The real explanation is stranger than either guess, since it depends on a force so weak that a single instance of it could not hold up a grain of sand, let alone a lizard.

For a long time this seemed to demand some kind of trick: a sticky secretion, perhaps, left behind wherever the foot touched, or thousands of microscopic suction cups pressed flat against the glass. Both explanations turn out to be wrong. Wipe a gecko's foot clean and press it to glass and it grips exactly as well as before, which rules out any residue. Place it in a sealed chamber with the air pumped out, removing any possibility of suction, and the grip holds just as strongly. The real explanation is stranger than either guess, since it depends on a force so weak that a single instance of it could not hold up a grain of sand, let alone a lizard.

lines.html: The gecko's foot is covered in ridges of hair-like structures called setae, each thinner than a human hair and packed so densely that a single toe carries roughly half a million of them. Under a microscope, every seta splits at its tip into hundreds of even finer branches, called spatulae, each one flattened like a tiny paddle only a few hundred nanometers across. It is at this scale, far below anything the unaided eye could resolve, that the actual grip takes place. When a spatula presses close enough to a surface, the electrons orbiting its atoms and the electrons in the surface's atoms begin to tug at one another, forming a weak attraction known as a van der Waals force. No glue, no moisture, and no muscular clamping are involved at all; the same attraction exists, faintly, between almost any two surfaces brought close enough together, whether or not either one is alive.

It is at this scale, far below anything the unaided eye could resolve, that the actual grip takes place. When a spatula presses close enough to a surface, the electrons orbiting its atoms and the electrons in the surface's atoms begin to tug at one another, forming a weak attraction known as a van der Waals force. lines.html: A single van der Waals attraction is almost nothing, far too faint to notice in ordinary life. What makes the gecko's grip strong is sheer number. Multiplied across hundreds of millions of spatulae spread over all four feet, these countless weak pulls add up to an adhesive force many times the gecko's own body weight, more than enough to let it hang from a single toe. Researchers who have measured this directly, by attaching tiny force sensors to a gecko's foot as it clings to a glass plate and gently pulling until the grip releases, have recorded forces strong enough that a sheet of spatulae the size of a human hand, if such a thing existed, could theoretically support the weight of an adult person.

lines.html: The gecko does not simply mash its foot against a surface and stay stuck forever, which would make climbing impossible rather than easy. Instead it engages and releases its grip with each step, angling its toes to bring the spatulae into close contact on the way down and peeling them away, a fraction of a degree at a time, on the way up. That peeling angle turns out to matter enormously: press a seta straight down against a surface and it grips fiercely, but tilt it back past a certain point, roughly thirty degrees in most studies, and the same structure releases almost instantly, with barely any effort at all. A gecko crossing a ceiling is, in effect, constantly attaching and detaching millions of microscopic hooks in a single fluid motion, fast enough that the whole process looks, to a human eye, like nothing more than an ordinary walk.

Explanation: The image of "the tired one dropping back a length" while another bird slides "up to cut the wind" shows the birds continually swapping positions, directly illustrating that no single goose holds the lead for long.


A. Incorrect: This line describes wings riding lift, not the shifting of leadership itself.


B. Incorrect: This line describes porch lights in town, unrelated to the geese's leadership.


C. Correct: The image of "the tired one dropping back" while another slides "up to cut the wind" directly shows the birds continually swapping positions, illustrating that leadership constantly shifts.


D. Incorrect: This line reflects the speaker's earlier misunderstanding of the geese's departure, not their shifting leadership.

Every morning, dozens of students at Alder Hollow Middle School arrive on bicycles, and most of them end up leaning their bikes against the fence by the gym doors because there is nowhere else to put them. (2) When the parent group first raised the idea of a real bike rack two years ago, they spoke with the office staff about the fence, and they never got a clear answer about whether the request was even being considered. (5) Two more bikes were knocked over and damaged during a windstorm the same month.

Explanation: The clause "biking is not for everyone" and the clause about students preferring the bus are both complete sentences, so joining them with only a comma creates a comma splice; a semicolon correctly separates the two independent clauses, while dropping the comma, adding "however" after a comma, or doubling the comma all leave the clauses improperly joined.


A. Incorrect: Removing all punctuation between the two independent clauses creates a run-on sentence.


B. Incorrect: Adding "however" after only a comma still leaves two independent clauses joined by nothing stronger than a comma, so the splice remains.


C. Incorrect: Doubling the comma with "and," still doesn't correctly join the two independent clauses.


D. Correct: A semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses without creating a splice or a run-on.

lines.text: Excerpt from "The Case for More Bike Parking at Alder Hollow"
lines.html: Excerpt from "The Case for More Bike Parking at Alder Hollow"

lines.text: by Student Author
lines.html: by Student Author

Every morning, dozens of students at Alder Hollow Middle School arrive on bicycles, and most of them end up leaning their bikes against the fence by the gym doors because there is nowhere else to put them. (2) When the parent group first raised the idea of a real bike rack two years ago, they spoke with the office staff about the fence, and they never got a clear answer about whether the request was even being considered. (3) The gym doors themselves are painted dark green to match the school's colors. (4) Last spring, three bikes were stolen from the fence in a single week. (5) Two more bikes were knocked over and damaged during a windstorm the same month.

(2) When the parent group first raised the idea of a real bike rack two years ago, they spoke with the office staff about the fence, and they never got a clear answer about whether the request was even being considered. (3) The gym doors themselves are painted dark green to match the school's colors. (4) Last spring, three bikes were stolen from the fence in a single week. (5) Two more bikes were knocked over and damaged during a windstorm the same month.

lines.html: (6) A covered bike rack near the main entrance would solve both problems at once. (7) The rack would give students a sturdy metal frame to lock their bikes to. (8) A simple roof would keep seats and gears dry during rainy mornings. (9) Riverbend Elementary, a school in our own district, installed a covered rack two years ago, and bike ridership there have nearly doubled since, according to a count the front office took each September.

(8) A simple roof would keep seats and gears dry during rainy mornings. (9) Riverbend Elementary, a school in our own district, installed a covered rack two years ago, and bike ridership there have nearly doubled since, according to a count the front office took each September.

lines.html: (10) Some administrators worry that a bike rack is an expense the school cannot justify right now. (11) The district's own facilities office estimates the cost of a twenty-space covered rack at under two thousand dollars, less than the school spends on hallway floor wax in a single year. (12) That is a small price for a change that could get more students moving safely under their own power instead of adding to the carpool line outside the office every morning. (13) A parent-teacher group has even offered to cover part of the cost through a fall fundraiser if the school commits to the project this year.

(13) A parent-teacher group has even offered to cover part of the cost through a fall fundraiser if the school commits to the project this year.

lines.html: (14) Other students point out that biking is not for everyone, students living far from school or on busy roads may reasonably prefer the bus or a ride from a parent. (15) No one is proposing that biking replace those options. (16) The goal is simply to make biking safe and practical for the students who already choose it, rather than leaving them to guess where an unwatched bike might still be standing at the end of the day. (17) A covered rack costs little, solves a problem families have raised for two years, and rewards students who are already doing exactly what the school claims to want: getting to school under their own power.
